en: Śrī Padyavāhinī (The Lamp of Śambhu’s Determination). Padyavāhinī.
Formerly, it was taught by the Guru known as Vyutpala;
therefore, the practice of ritual action must be performed in every way.
The Lord of Yogins, purifying the earth with his feet, [composed this work].
Then, by that same effort, he compiled the five currents;
among them, there exist manuals (paddhatis) that have been arranged in various fragments.
The [sections] beginning with "Śrīśāmbhavodaya" and so forth are colored by various names;
because the extraction of mantras, meditations, sandhyā rites, nyāsas, worship, and so on,
are employed here and there [in different forms], they cannot be made uniform.
By those who are dull-witted, devoid of intelligence, and lacking in service to their gurus;
therefore, seeking the welfare of all, he remained in the position of a disciple to that [teacher].
Parameṣṭhin, having carefully meditated upon the heart of his guru, [declares]:
"This certain brahmin Śaṅkara, free from passion and possessed of discerning intellect,
composes a manual in verse that flows as a single stream."
In reality, the very sequence of time is the life-force (jīva) of action.
Since only that which possesses sequence can possess sequence here, how could duality possibly arise?
Sequence is simply this: "this is before that," or "this is after that."
He alone is Śiva, the one who ensures the absence of confusion in the sequence [of ritual acts],

through the arrangement of mantras and mandalas, recitation, meditation, worship, and so forth; as well as by means of mudrās, [the invocation (āvāhana),] the offering of oblations (balyudvāsana), and libations (tarpaṇa).
He who is renowned for his sequence in sacrifice and is celebrated as the foremost performer should rise early in the morning with a serene mind and dwell facing the east.
With palms joined in reverence, he should recite the three *śrīpādukās* for the venerable Guru.
Having meditated upon the moon at the vital point of the earth with mindfulness, one should invoke Gaṇeśa (Heramba).
With the six long vowels, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) upon the [six] classes, faces, hands, and limbs.
The elephant-faced one is white; he holds a mouse, an axe, a tusk, a water-pot, and a trident.
One who eats first [after the ritual] shall pacify all obstacles by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
At this time, having recited according to one's capacity, one should dissolve [the deity] along with its ancillaries (aṅga) into the heart—
that which consists of the unsurpassed Great Breath, the Point (bindu), the Sound (nāda), and the Creative Energy (kalā).
One should contemplate three times the great mantra of great heroism, which is the sovereignty of consciousness,
within the flower of knowledge (*vidyāpuṣpa*), which is white and foremost, and radiant as a great sacred seat (*mahāpīṭha*).
Likewise, in the maṇḍala, in the sacrificial vessel (caruka), and similarly within the seat of mantra (mantrapīṭha),
as well as in the various mudrās, one should join the four great seats (mahāpīṭha) and the Great State (mahāpada) beginning with Prakāśānandanātha.
The white foot is enclosed within the tridents of breath (prāṇa), moon, and fire;
following this sequence beginning with the red [foot] and so forth, it is joined with Parā and Aparā in the *Prakāśinī*.
The red foot is remembered as being encapsulated by the seed-syllables beginning with Bhṛgu.

*Emmāyā hrī* * * * * * phaṭ hlauṃ—this is the pentad of the Praṇavas. The Śāmbhava and Āṇava [mantras] are joined internally in both direct and reverse order. One should meditate on the two feet as being like those of one born that very day, situated within the cavity of the feet.
By joining the tips of the little finger, the thumb, the index finger, and the middle finger,
one should offer the five services (pañcopacārakān) through the elements of earth, ether, fire, and water, along with perfume,
flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings as is appropriate.

At the conclusion of the worship with the Praṇavas, one should offer the *yoni-añjali*. Having worshipped with the seven *upacāra* offerings... [and] having worshipped with the mode of absorption (*laya-vṛtti*), one should [offer] into the heart with the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
In that same manner, one should place the pair of lotus-feet of one’s own guru upon the crown of the head.
* * * * * * * * * * * Śvāvulapulī.
Candragarbha is the portion of Bālin; the one called Muktā is joined with Mahilā.
Lalita is Śaṅkha and Karuṇe; Kaṇṭha was formerly another Kaṇṭha.
Kumāra is joined with Sahajā; Ratnadevī... [is]... *Note: The text provided contains an ellipsis (* * * *). The translation reflects the available portion.*
Yuktapratiṣṭha is joined with Sahajā;
Cidākhya is joined with the fearless Śivā and joined with Sahajā;
Śrīkaṇṭha is joined with Vidyā; and Śrīśiva is joined with Sahajā.
Śrīnaṭa, endowed with creative intuition; Kumāra, accompanied by Sahajā;
and those ending with Caryā and Naṭanātha—these are remembered as the eighteen Gurus.
In the Śāmbhava teaching, the formula "I worship the Pādukā" should be appended at the end of each name.
Having performed the ritual service and taken [the mantra] to heart, one should contemplate a hexagon within the cavity.
Between the mantras of the God and the Goddess, there are rays at the tips of the flavors (the six directions).
[These consist of] Nāda, Śukla, Antya, Viṣa, Bhū, Jala, Āgni, Arcis, and Bindu.
Having extracted the *rasātman* mantra, one should recite it as long as life lasts.
5) Among those [mantras] beginning with *vāgbhava*, there are three consisting of *dyuti*, *dīrgha*, *dyuti*, *māyā*, and *indu*.
Likewise, the syllable *krodha* (kṣa) joined with the subtle (*sūkṣma*, i), two syllables from the middle of the *ṛti* group (ṛ and ṝ),

the letter ending in *la* (la) joined with *repha* (ra), the pair of tortoises (kūrmayugala, ka and kha) joined with the womb (*yonisaṃyuta*, m), and the fourth *tāra* (the nasal bindu) as its crown— this ten-syllable mantra becomes great.
In both [forms], they are seated in the lotus posture (padmāsana) upon the head of the *puṣṭa* [mantra], bestowing the world;
in the other [form], the two are dancing, bestowing the fruits of all desires.
At the end of the *praṇava* in direct order (*anuloma*), there is the *kūṭa* beginning with *ha* and ending with *ramā*.

At the end of Navātmānandanātha, one should extract the mantra of the *daśā*, then the syllable *Ramā*. Joined with the *niṣkalā* and the *mahāyukta*, one should extract the foot along with the *samayā*. Then, in reverse order from the *abbaprā* [mantra], there is the pentad of *praṇavas*.
In the Śāmbhava [tradition], one worships the sandals ending with Ekavidyā.
One should worship the rays known as Earth, Water, Fire, Air, and Ether, along with the Mind,
ending with the Bindu, in sequence, using the syllables *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ha*, *sa*.
One should place a group of four, a group of five (or six), a group of four, and a group of five;
then, in the six corners, one should assign the twenty-eight rays starting from the east,
conjoined with the names of the powers such as Oḍḍī, Jālā, Pūrṇā, and Kāmā.
One should visualize four [mantras] enclosed by the seed-syllables of the [five] elements within the lamp-stand:
Śrīkaṇṭha with Gaganānanda in the heavenly realm, Śaṅkara in the mortal world, the one named Kapiṅga with Pātālā, and Sadyojāta joined with Nāgayā.
The five [syllables] are encapsulated by *vaṃ*, and likewise the six are encapsulated by *ra*.
Ānanda is joined with Hākinī, while Āvalī is joined with Rākinī.
The Lord is the sovereign... [at the time of] death.
... Hākinī resides in the six [petals] within the radiant [center]. The support is joined with Raktā, and the Lord of the Wheel is united with Caṇḍā.
One should join Kuraṅgīśa, Karālākhya, Madaṅghrīśa, and Mahocchuṣā,
encased within the seed-syllable of Samīra;
having performed the ritual service (*upacarya*) and made it reside in the heart, one should recite the mantra of the supreme fire of Śrī.
[The mantra] accompanied by the letter *ra*...
Then the Guru, likewise himself acting as the Guru, should [perform the rite].
Thereafter, one should join the ninefold *ra*-soul at the end of the venerable Lord Guru.
Tārā, Māyā, Kāmadughā, Amoghā, Varadā, and likewise Daśāntāraṅgasambuddhi...
Thus ends the great mantra of the *Kulasaṃyuktakāmadhenu*,
the great mantra of Śrī Heramba, according to the lineage of one's own guru.
Then follows the *Navadaśāraśmiparapāvakakāmadhuk*.
Having performed the preliminary service, one should meditate upon the venerable Lord Śrīparābhaṭṭāraka.
Having uttered in sequence "Māyā," "Lakṣmī," the king of the letters of the great mantra, and the Bindu, and having recited the Mātṛkā, one should say: "I am the Sovereign of the Vowels, the Glory."
One should thus utter the Māyā, the Śākta, the Lamp, and the Mātṛkā;
with Bhṛgu, Īśa, Vyāpinī, and the letters beginning with Ka, [one utters] the Heart of the Lord Śrīparā.
The first three short vowels are for creation, and the eleventh vowel is for disease.
One should dissolve the thirty-three consonants from *ka* to *kṣa* in sequence into Bhṛgu and Īśa. With kicks, slaps, and upturned faces—
terribly terrifying with the radiance between the fragments of Bhṛgu at the end of the creation-king— one should perform the dissolution.
First, one should perform three claps (tāla) for the pacification of the flood of obstacles that cause division.
Having placed the moving Ambikā upon the five locations— the head, face, heart, secret place, and feet—
and having formed the thumb-and-crest (aṅguṣṭha-śikhā) mudrā, one should recite [the mantra] twenty-seven times.

One should bind [the letters] in the sequence of the ten directions using the vowels ending in *sparśa* (the semi-vowels) conjoined with the earth (*kṣma*). Having repeatedly drawn that which is to be measured by the self of Bhṛgu (the letter *ha*) within the measure of the trident (*śūla*), one should forcefully write it in one's own northern Śiva.
One should contemplate Śrī Parārtha, who is firmly established in the non-duality of Śrī Parā;
he is white and reddish at his extremities, and wise in the states of emanation and maintenance.
Then, one should join [the mantra] with *nitye*, *pūrṇe*, and the wife of Fire (*svāhā*) at the heart. Next,
one should extract the third part using the words *repha-bindu-mahā-pūrva*, *saṃhāriṇi*, *kṛśe*,
and the words *caṇḍikā-ha-anta-netra-astra*.

One should recollect the great seed-mantra of the self, which is the essence of the seven-fold Lord Śrī, [composed] with the letter *ra*, the vital breath (*ha*), the moon (*sa*), water (*va*), fire (*ra*), the fourth vowel (*ī*), and the bindu. Then, in the Mahānākhyam, one should utter the phrase "Ananta-bhāskara."
One should extract the mantra-word of the weapon (astra) ending with *mahādiccaṇḍakāhāntanetra*.
This meaning consists of four human [syllables] joined in both direct and reverse order.
One should contemplate the needle sequentially from below, to the middle, and upwards.
Then, one should reflect upon the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in the reverse order.

The knower of mantras, through the processes of emanation and so forth, should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) by means of both direct and reverse orders upon the root, the heart, the gates, the apertures of the sun, and the skull, which are the uprooters [of duality].

One should bind the Bhairavī-mudrā in the belly with the seven syllables (*saptapiṇḍa*). Dissolution (*laya*) is one among the four [stages] as taught in the scriptures of the Trika and Mahārtha. On the head, one should draw a white [triangle] and so forth.
The right side of the heart, situated in the midst of the swans, is the support of the Kula as declared by Śiva.
One should contemplate the consciousness of Śiva by means of the Mātṛkā in reverse order;
[one should contemplate it] in forward order... [as follows].
Then Paraśivānanda, followed by the supreme Kāmeśvarī;
then the Divine Current (divyaugha) and the Great Current (mahaugha), and thereafter Sarvaprajñāmbikā.
In the sevenfold teaching, the Divine Current (divyaugha) ends with Prakāśānandanātha.
Even within the Divine [Current], there is the manifold [tradition] of Kauvalyadevī and Ambāmahas;
as for the Fused Current (siddhaugha), there is no fixed number here among humans.
Cidviśva, Śaktipūrveśa, Kamala, Athamanohara, Paramasvātman, Pratibhāmṛta,
the one called Vidyā, Naṭa, Nāda, and Kumāra as the thirteenth.
Having performed the preliminary worship, one should place [the mantra] in the heart with the *Śrīsaubhāgyahṛdaya*.
One should extract the *Vāgbhava* syllable consisting of the letters from *vyoma* (ha) to *kṣa*, ending with *ambā* (i).
The limbs [of the mantra] are produced by means of *nāda* (ḥ), the moon (i), one's own earth (la), the vital breath (ha), *kṣā* (kṣa), and *māyā* (hrīṃ).
"By means of the *māyās* of Soma, Svayambhū, and Rasita, one should extract the Power (*śakti*).

Thus has the root-vidyā of Tripurasundarī been declared by Śiva. One should practice [this] from the base (*mūla*) up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*). (One should practice the *vilāda* from the base upward.)
Through the recitation of the mantras for burning and flooding, and by means of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath,
one should contemplate the body, the senses, and the world as pervaded by a mass of light from that [mantra].
One should contemplate the consciousness of glorious prosperity, which is joined with the *saubhāgyavidyā*.
The Kāmarāja [bīja] is formed by the syllables *kro*, *ḍī*, *śa*, *bhū*, *pra*, *ti*, *ṣṭhā*, *kṣa*, *bi*, and *ndu*.
The Vāgbhava [bīja] is well-established with the syllables *va*, *rṇa*, *rā*, *ḍyō*, *ni*, *bi*, and *ndu*.
One should utter the Śākta [seed-syllable] by means of those known as Ghora, Indu, and Śūla to invoke Sampatkarī.
Having thus pronounced the triad of seed-syllables, one should also complete it in reverse order,
according to the sequence of Kāma, Vāgbhava, and Kaivalya, both in direct and inverse form.
I worship my own self-reflection (*svavimarśa*), whose measure is fashioned by a *kalā*.
After the procedure for the *prabhāvi* [initiation], one should go outside to perform the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*).
Having performed the necessary purifications, such as cleansing and the preliminary brushing of the teeth.
Having consecrated seven times with water held in the palm of the right hand— water empowered by the seed-syllables of the great elements, earth and the rest, adorned with the *bindu*—
one should sprinkle it three times on the head using all the tips of the fingers of the left hand.
Having filled the remaining light-filled [breath] through the left nostril until it reaches the heart,
one should burn this darkness-filled [impurity] upon the stone of Śiva’s vajra and cast it out through the right [nostril] with the weapon-mantra; this ritual act is the *aghamarṣaṇa*.
One should bathe three times with the *saubhāgyasampad* and *vidyā* mantras using [cow] urine;

one should perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) twice and then commence the twilight ritual (*sandhyā*) by reciting the *jyeṣṭhā* mantra from the root abode (*mūlālaya*) three times each, beginning with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*.
One should worship her who is yellow in color, three-eyed, adorned [with ornaments],
and whose right and left lotus-hands hold the gestures of supreme fearlessness (*parābhaya*) and a skull, as well as a serpent.
*Hrāṃ*, encapsulated by the seed-syllable, [is] Jyeṣṭhā...
[the Bhairavas].
In the *Pañcatārā-sitāṅgādibhairavānanda-nāṭaka*:
Caṇḍakaumārī and the Krodhabhairavas,
Vaiṣṇavī and likewise the two Unmattas, Vārāhī and Kapālika.
Indrāṇībhīṣaṇa and Ādimuṇḍāsaṃhārabhairava [are worshipped],
and then Mahālakṣmī is worshipped at midday with her left limb.
She is sprinkled with the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* and seated upon the moon-throne at the navel-center (*nābhicakra*).
She bears two rosaries of beads and two beautiful books.

Having uttered the seed-syllable *hrīṃ* enclosed within *hlauṃ*, followed by [the name] ending in the dative case (*vāmāyai*) enclosed between them, one should perform the ritual services (*upacāra*) and so forth as before.
One should meditate on her as red in color, arisen from the seed-syllable *hrauṃ* at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*;
she stands in the center of a circle of fire, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with beautiful ornaments.
In her right hands, she holds a trident, the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*), a skull-cup, and likewise a raised index finger (*tarjanī*).
And on the left side, she should be visualized as before, with the ritual services (upacāra) and so forth.
With the seed-syllable *hrauṃ* enclosed [by the name], and Raudrī likewise enclosed within that,
one should perform the libation to Bhairava and others in the dative case, as previously described.

One should likewise sprinkle her three times with the *saubhāgyasampad* and *vidyā* mantras; she should be visualized as holding the ritual offerings and so forth on her left side, as previously described.
Having offered the *arghya* three times each, and having completed a hundred [offerings] in the mandala,
one should then recite both the *gāyatrī* mantras and the two *vidyās*.
To the wise one who moves within the lineage, and to the golden ones, [one offers] the three fluids.
At the end of "keśāya dhīmahi," [one says] "tannaḥ śambhuḥ pracodayāt. At the end of "kulakaulini vidvānte" and "he mahāmālini," having uttered up to "dhīmahi," [one says] "tannaḥ kubji pracodayāt."
One should perform the bathing, twilight rites, and so forth within the heart by means of the Heart-mantra of the New [Trika],
and likewise place the two Vidyās within one's own heart by means of their respective Heart-mantras. Thus it was taught by Śaṅkara, the embodied disciple of the venerable Somānanda.
When the *padyavāhinī* has been performed, the first flow is complete.
Having reached a secluded place, the self-controlled practitioner should dwell facing the east.
Having requested permission from the Guru, he should begin before him the entire practice of *nyāsa*.

If one firmly presses the palm of the left hand with the tips of the fingers of the right hand and directs the movement of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth from the fat [of the abdomen] up to the root of the thighs,
and likewise from the base up to the heart; ||| 105 ||
From the region of the navel up to the ears, the heart, and the crown of the head—
one should clearly contemplate the locations of the five great elements starting from the ears.
One should dissolve the yellow, white, red, orange, and dark-blue [elements], each with its own maṇḍala,
by means of the five *tāra* syllables together with their respective seed-syllables;
that is, each preceding great element into each succeeding one.
Having dissolved the elements that constitute the body according to the reasoning already stated,
one of purified intellect should perform the cremation while consciousness remains as the sole residue.
[One should visualize] the Mūlādhāra, rising from the space between the anus and the genitals, with the brilliance of lightning.
All splendor is grounded in [him]...
by him alone is knowledge [attained]... the Lord of Consciousness is absolute sovereignty.
The inseparability of that power of consciousness is established through many philosophical systems.
Therefore, the gurus deliberate; it cannot be determined [otherwise].
like female serpents, having kissed the Self known as the *bodhaliṅga*, which is full sovereignty.
She has determined that everything is the delusion of the construction of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).
One should awaken her— who is greedily intent on the full enjoyment of savoring the internal experience of the *mātṛkā*s—
by means of the Guru’s word, she who possesses a radiance blazing like ten million fires of cosmic destruction (*kālāgni*).
Having raised [the breath] with the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ), one should lead it into the Suṣumnā.
With a tongue that flashes like ten million lightning bolts and is constantly licking [the palate],
one should [unite] Sākinī— whose name consists of the letters *sa-ṣa-va-ra*— in the Mūlādhāra (with the heart).
[She is] the *Kākinī* who possesses six petals in the *laṃ*, *ra*, *ya*, *ma*, *bha*, and *ba*;
she is surrounded by the letters *pha*, *pa*, *na*, *tha*, *da*, *tha*, *ta*, *ṇa*, *ḍḍha*, and *ḍā* in the *Maṇipūra*.
One should meditate on Lākinī, situated upon a ten-petaled lotus in the heart, and Rākinī upon a twelve-petaled lotus in the solar plexus;
she is encircled by the syllables ṭha, ṭha, ña, ja, jha, cha, ca, ai, aṅ, agha, ga, kha, ka, and va.
Then, one should meditate on Ḍākinī in the sixteen-spoked lotus at the throat center (viśuddhi).

Having brought under one's own control the *Ājñā* [cakra], which is encircled by the vowels and possesses the functions known as *Sarga*, *Indu*, *Sandhi*, *Klība*, *Śrotra*, and *Netra*, within the lotus of the two petals of *Ha* and *Kṣa*; and then, having likewise mastered *Hākinī*, who is the Mother (*Ambikā*) of *Bindu* and *Nāda*.
Having tasted the nectar of the supreme point (parabindu) situated at the end of the twelve [finger-breadths],
and having for some time unweariedly expanded the state of the *ḍāmara*,
he experienced non-dual unity within the great ocean of the elixir (*rasāyana*).
Having bathed the body along with its support by means of the cool-natured stream of nectar residing in that moon, one performs withdrawal in reverse order; then,
as the supreme bindu, one is emitted into the sky of the heart within the body of the power of emanation.
One should unite one's own self there and contemplate the form of Śambhu. With the *navātman* mantra joined with the six long vowels, one should place [the mantras] upon the fingers;
and with the six limbs joined with the seed-syllables (*jāti*), one should place them upon the six faces with their respective faces.
By means of the [syllables] of the west, north, south, east, and above— the outermost ones—
along with the fourth *praṇava* situated within the *samaya*,
there is the three-limbed [mantra] of the two lords of the *daśā* through the conjunction of the sixth vowel (*rasa*), the musical note (*svara*), and the genus (*jāti*) with the faces (*vaktra*).
With the primary and secondary offerings, triple-strung and elaborated,
one should present the internal peace-offering (*antaśśantibali*) for the sake of pacifying the defects of division.
Having visualized a four-cornered mandala marked with a circle in its center,
and having placed the Vāgbhava syllable within it followed by the word "vyāpaka," one should mentally worship it once with the mantra "maṇḍalāya."
One should conceive of the feet as the base extending up to the ears, and the head as the vessel.
One should conceive of the entire range of the senses as the *argha* (offering water),
and the water as filled by uninterrupted consciousness.
One should remember the *vargādi*, *bhṛṅgu*, and *malā* mantras;
then the *dhruva*, the *māyā*, all the words [ending with] "to all obstructors," and "to the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*), followed by *hūṃ*.

* * * * * * * by means of the two external [channels] * * * * । * * * * * * * one should also observe the lotus-faced one (*padmānana*). * One should perceive him in the cavity (*bila*), the forehead (*lalāṭa*), the eye (*akṣi*), the face (*vadana*), and the throat (*gala*).

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the *kūṭa* [mantra] with colored powders: yellow on the heart, dark blue at the destruction [of the body], smoky-grey at the anus, and the color of the sun (yellow) at the feet; it is yellow throughout all the limbs.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the nine [mantras] beginning with Ambā on the heart, throat, face, arms, and head— where the hair-whorls turn clockwise on all limbs— in order to attain stability of the body.
Having recited the limbs of the two deities as before, one should offer libations three times each.
One should place *sa-jūṃ* on the surface of the crown-lock (*cūḍātala*) and *ṅ* in the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
One should place the seed-syllable *kha-ṭa-ka-sa-ha-gha-ra-yūṃ* on the forehead; *sa-ha-kṣrūṃ* on the right temple (*dakṣaśaṅkha*), and *kṣa-ra-la-u-oṃ* on the left.
*Hasa phreṭ* at the edge of the right eyebrow; *sa hrūṃ* on the edge of the left eyebrow;
*sūṃ* at the *bindu*; *saṃ* on the tongue; *hrīṃ* at the root of the palate; *kṣa rakṣrūṃ* at the *phaṭ*; *sa haṃ* at the two ears; *la ma ya rūṃ* at the two temples (*urakūpaka*).
One should place *hasūṃ* on the stalk of the throat and *ḍayatūṃ* on the secret part of the throat.
*Ñayatūṃ* and *auṃḍayāya* are placed on the breasts, starting from the front portion.
*Has* is for the armor of the breast, and *jūṃ* is for the wrapping of the left breast.
One should place *saklīṃ* and *eṃ* on the two armpits, and *hasaum* at the navel.

One should place *hraḥ phreṭ* on the palms of the hands, and *sahrīṃ hrauṃ* on the tip and base of the *liṅga*. One should place *bhreṃ* on the fat, and one should contemplate *pheṃ* on the right testicle.
The practitioner should place *haṃ* on the left side of the waist-thread (*dhātṛsūtraka*);
he should place *hasapharayūṃ* in the region of the anus;
and he should place *hasapharūṃ* and *hakṣrauṃ* on the sides of the rectum.
The seed-syllable *hrauṃ* should be in the path of the wind; *jhrāṃ* and *hrūṃ* are in the two wheels of the knees;
one should visualize *ḍahūauṃ* and *harakṣrauṃ* in the pair of shanks.
One should place *vraṃ yaraṃ* on the pair of ankles, *harakṣaphaṭ* below,
and *naphayarīṃ jajhakṣaharauṃ* on the two gateways of the anus. One should also place *hasarūṃha haraphaṭ* on the soles of the feet.
Then, one should visualize the seed-syllable *laṃ hrīṃ* on the bone of the spine. One should place *jaḥ sahasa jūṃ kṣaṃ* on both sides.
One should place *ha ra phaṭaṃ sa hīṃ* on the two elbows, and *ga sa ma pa na lūṃ* on the right wrist.
One should place the seed-syllable *la-vaya-ra-has* on the left wrist;
then one should place *hasa-phreṃ-kṣa-phaṭ-kṣa-rūṃ* on the two shoulders;
and one should also place *phreṃ-ca-kṣa-maya-rūṃ* on both nipples.
One should place the triad *haraphaṭapharīṃ*, *kṣrauñca*, and *ha* [in the three eyes]; *cakṣuṣyaṃ* and *prāṇasāraṃ* in the two pupils;
and the tetrad *hrūṃ*, *hasakalarahrīṃ*, *a*, and *kakṣrūñca*.
At the two junctions of the ring fingers and the thumbs, and at the bases of the two middle fingers...
[omitted] ...from the feet up to the head, [one should perform the ritual] once each with the letters from *ma* to *kṣa*.

This placement of the sixteen seeds is performed once upon the heart with the *mātṛkā*. Having placed the seed-syllables, one should sequentially place the stream of letters upon the root [genitals], the heart, the mouth, and the head, during the morning, midday, evening, and midnight respectively.
Through various metaphorical expressions and literal meanings, the pair of mantras is distinct;
she has the form of fresh rain clouds, dances, and is endowed with youth.
Her left foot has its big toe touching [the ground], while her right is in the *argha-paryaṅka* posture;
she is adorned with a great conch, a jewel, a discus, a lotus, and a skin;
her hips are marked by a dagger and a torch, and she is decorated with a human skull.
Having five faces and twelve eyes, with hair as coarse as that of a barbarian standing erect,
she holds in her left hands the skull-bowl, the trident, the discus, and the banner; and in her right hands, for the sake of the liberation of the world, she bears the weapons of Śambhu.

In the cremation ground, she is surrounded by deities with palms joined in reverence; her face is always smiling, she constantly destroys fear through her recitation, and she is adorned with *pāribhadra* flowers that possess the fragrance of the foot of Brahmā.
To the left of that [deity], one should meditate upon the Goddess, who is graceful in her dance;
for the attainment of all goals, one should visualize her as red and exceedingly slender,
holding a staff of Brahmā in her right hand and a trident in her left.
For the two arms and for recitation (*japa*) and so forth, one should visualize the Goddess Jagatsutā in the lotus posture (*padmāsana*).
For the sake of enjoyment, one should visualize the blue-colored Nīlā, adorned with a garland of severed heads, as having a gross body.
Both [the hands] are in the head-position (*śiraḥkrama*) [in the manuscript], while the two [feet] are in the lotus posture, bestowing the world.

In another [form], there are two dancing [deities] who bestow the fruits of all desires. Having recited the ancillary mantras ten times the number of the root mantra, one should cause them to dissolve into the heart.
Now follows the *sampatkarī* ritual placement (*nyāsa*) at the *mūlādhāra*, moistened with the story (*kathā*).
Through the conjunction of the five seed-syllables— māyā (hrīṃ), manmatha (klīṃ), vāk (aiṃ), blūṃ, and strīṃ—
the syllables hrīṃ and klīṃ are placed within the navel hexagon, while blūṃ and strīṃ surround them on the outside.
One should contemplate the common Haṃsa seated upon the Kāmayantra throne;
first uttering "I am He," one should then [offer] the word for the Self of the Universe,
and the mantra ending with "Śivakāmāya namaḥ."

The state arising from the knowledge of the form of emanation belongs to the Self in the form of consciousness. "Salutation to Sampat-sarasvatī"—this is the twenty-six-syllable mantra. With this, one should worship the Goddess with the seed-syllables... [and so forth].
One should place [the syllables]:
khaṃ, gaṃ, ghaṃ, ṅaṃ, chaṃ, jaṃ, jhaṃ, ñaṃ, ṭaṃ, ṭhaṃ, ḍaṃ, ḍhaṃ, ṇaṃ; thus [is] the direction. In particular, one should resort to haṃ.
One should first practice with "so'ham," and at its end, for the Taijasa-ātman,
the fourteen-syllable mantra ending with "śivakāmāya.
[One should worship] the Goddess seated upon his lap, who is the presiding deity of the Vāgbīja.
For the conceptualization of the form of stability, which is of the nature of consciousness in its primordial state,
the goddess Sarasvatī is the mantra consisting of twenty-six syllables.
Having recited this seed-mantra ten times as a ritual service, one should lead [the disciple] into the cave.
One should contemplate the great lotus of the syllable *MĀ*, which has the form of the pericarp of the wheel of speech.
Then, one should place it upon the head, outside of the pericarp, just as [one did] for the heart.
Outside of that is a sixteen-petaled lotus of vowels, devoid of the filaments.
There is also a lotus of vowels beginning with *klaṃ* and *krāṃ*, along with *saṃ* and *sām*.
Then there is a thirty-two-petaled lotus beginning with *ha-sa-ka-iṃ* and ending with *ha-sa-sa-iṃ*.
Outside, there is one petal marked with the syllable Oṃ, and further outside, one petal marked with the syllable Ha.
At the end, for the sake of the Self of Wisdom (prājñātman), the eternal [syllable Dhruva] is placed; then, for the sake of Śiva’s desire, the heart [syllable Hrīṃ] follows.
With this twelve-syllable mantra, one should contemplate the partless Haṃsa.
And [he should worship] the deity presiding over the seed-syllable *Śakti*, who is seated upon his lap;
the self of consciousness (*saṃvidātmā*) consisting of eighteen syllables, whose nature is dissolution and whose state is the non-discriminative deep sleep (*sauṣupta*).
With this [mantra], one should worship the seed-syllable ten times within the hollow of the lotus-casket (*abjasampuṭa*).

Having meditated upon the Goddess as one's own self— colored by the shower of nectar that is the outflow of the aforementioned recollection— one should perform [the practice] with the inhalation and exhalation of the breath,
from the aperture (bilam) up to the root, and from the root up to the Brahma-aperture.
One should recite the root-vidyā for as long as one deems appropriate for the time.
For the sake of attaining stability in a body created from nectar,
one should draw [the syllables] into their respective locations by means of the fifty syllables and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should place [the letters] upon the throat, the two eyes, the ears and nostrils,

the pair of lips, the ends of the two eyebrows, the head, and the tips of the tongue, using the vowels; and like the hands, one should place them on the forehead, the sides, the back, the navel, and the belly, joined with the diphthongs.
One should perform the placement with the letters of touch upon those located at the heart, the armpits, and the back;
likewise on the left hand, the two feet, and the lower and upper hands.
One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) in sequence with the letters from *a* to *kṣa*.

On the teeth, one should place [the seed-syllables] using the letters *da*, *kṣa*, *ṇa*, *nirvṛtti* (the vowel *u*), and *manmatha* (the syllable *klīm*), together with the [five faces of Śiva]: Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta.
The fourth [placement] is on the heart, the thumbs and other fingers, and on the middle, ring, and little fingers, as well as on the palms of the hands;
one who is not impotent should perform this with the six long vowels combined with the mantras beginning with Manmatha (Kāmadeva) and ending with Jātyanta.
Having placed [the mantras] upon the ears and the crown of the head using the finger-mantras beginning with the thumb, which are endowed with five faces—
namely those designated as upward, eastern, southern, northern, and western—
one should meditate upon the *haṃsa* and the *ahaṃ*.
Through the application of the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should contemplate the Goddess as one's own self.
The creator, joined with creation, the progenitor, Bhṛgu, Caṇḍī, Niḥ, and Kara—
this is the seven-syllabled Vidyā, the sovereign of seventy million mantras.

One should meditate upon her holding a garland woven from flowers that are the mantras, numbering seventy million, which have emerged from the fierce *vidyā*-creepers; she resembles the rising sun, with the crescent moon shining upon her crown.

One should firmly begin the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) for the sake of achieving identity with her, who has three eyes and causes supreme fear. Having filled [the left nostril] with the seed-syllable (*bīja*) by means of the left [nostril], one should exhale it through the right at the end.
In the same way, one should fill with the right [nostril] and likewise exhale through the left;
having performed this three times with the two seed-syllables, one should perform six rotations in sequence.
The knower of yoga, having filled the channels with the seed-syllable *vaṃ* from the two voids (*kha*) and performing the retention (*kumbhaka*),
should remain for sixty-four measures while being drenched by the nectar flowing from the moon and sun situated at the end of the twelve fingers.

To stabilize the purified body, one should perform three rounds of breath control (prāṇāyāma) while reciting the root mantra (mūlavidyā) three times, accompanied by the utterances of the seed-syllables (bīja) in indistinct, distinct, and terrifying tones,
along with striking the heels on the ground, clapping the hands, and making loud facial expressions.
Then one should perform three claps and place [the mantras] upon the fingers.
With the syllables *nivṛtti*, *bindu*, *ananta*, *indu*, *śukla*, *śūla*, and *visarga*,
recited twice starting from the middle finger, one should again install the seat of the Self (*ātmasana*).
The pair of *māyā* and *lakṣmī* seed-syllables (*hrīṃ śrīṃ*) should be placed at the beginning of all mantras.

Then, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the mantra ending in *namaḥ*, according to the distinctions of the seats of *māyā*, *manmatha*, the third goddess (*tārttīyadevī*), and the self (*ātman*).

Having thus brought forth the words "vāksamanmatathārttīyaiḥ," the speech that masters vowels, *repha*, *bala*, and the *bindu* follows thereafter. This [mantra], ending with the deity-name and ending with the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), one should first place upon the head.
On the plowshare (phāla), *kavarga-kala-hrīṃ*; then Kāmeśī as before.
On the dot (*bindu*), with the consonant class (*varga*) and *hlīṃ*; then Modinī as before.
On the throat (*kaṇṭha*), *tavarga-ylūṃ*; then Vimalā as before.
In the heart, the *tavarga* [consonants], preceded by *śrīṃ* and then *aruṇā*;
at the navel, the *pavarga* [consonants], preceded by *hlam*, *hrūṃ*, and then *jayinī*.

At the base [of the feet], one should place the syllables beginning with *ya*, namely *jhrūṃ*, followed by the word *sarveśvarī*. Then, at the *vyāhṛti* [the navel], one should likewise place the syllables beginning with *va*, namely *kṣrīṃ*, and the goddess Kaulinī.
This placement of the eight deities of speech forcibly bestows the perfection of the deities.
"I take refuge in her who has the luster of the orb of the rising sun, who possesses four arms and three eyes,
and who holds a noose, a goad, arrows, and a bow.
Having meditated thus and performed the ritual services, one should then recite the mantra along with its ancillaries and dissolve it into the heart."
Through the unfolding of the absolute freedom of the consciousness of the Great Subject,
one should contemplate the liberating consciousness that is full of nectar.
After [the mantra] *māyā śrī smara tārā*, one should utter *namo bhagavati*.
Having said "O Annapūrṇā, mine," one should then state the desired object:
"Give me food. This mantra, ending with *dviṭha* (svāhā), consists of twenty-seven syllables.
One should place the fourfold seed-syllable and power-mantra (*bīja-śakti*) at the root, the heart, and the openings of the mouth.
Likewise, one should assign Bhuvana, Kamalā, Subhagā, and Parapūrvikā; at the end of the Vidyā and at the end of the Hṛdaya,
one should place [the goddesses] Brahmāṇī, Māheśī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and Bahurūpakā;
[they are] the eye, the sight, the four Vedas, the sight, the spirits, the sight, and the moment...
In this *Padyavāhinī* composed by Śaṅkara, the embodied disciple of Śrī Somānanda, the river of the *Pūrṇā* [has been brought] to its full flow.
When the equipment for the sacrifice is complete and the means have been perfected through the performance of the rite.
In a place crowded with canopies, rows of lamps, offerings of water (arghya), fourfold offerings, and so forth,
the self-controlled practitioner, facing east, should sit upon a seat provided with a pillow. Having requested permission from the Guru, he should first worship the Kula-sun.
In front, on one's left side, one should prepare the general *arghya* offering.
One should fashion an eight-petaled lotus and, with that water, a mandala for the *arghya*. Having drawn a square with four corners, one should place a vessel of rice upon its center.
Then, having performed the three-limbed rite with the second *praṇava* over the vessel of *arghya*,
one should worship it with the limbs (*aṅgas*). One should then worship Ananta upon the lotus-seat with the mantra "To Ananta," encased within [the syllables] of one's own chosen color.
From the center of the heart-lotus, having drawn out the red seed-syllable *hrauṃ* by means of the process of exhalation and established it outside, one worships Ananta and so forth.
[The deity holds] a trident and the gesture of fearlessness in the right hand, and a lotus and a bell in the left.
One should meditate upon oneself as the all-pervading, pot-bellied Lord, arisen from the center of the seed-syllable of Bhairava, the Sun of the Family (Kulārka).
[This occurs] within the seed-syllables consisting of the letter *ra*, the vital breath (*ha*), the moon (*sa*), the fire of dissolution (*ra*), the trident (*u*), and the moon (*i*).
And in the center, one should invoke the Kula-mārttaṇḍa with its dative case ending;
having worshipped him with these ritual services, one should worship the limbs of dissolution and enjoyment.
Then, having worshipped with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-mantra) and offered the food offering (naivedya), one should withdraw it into one's own seat.
Having offered three handfuls of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should offer the water of honor (arghya) into oneself,
together with the remaining drops from that [offering] and the previously used flowers from the floral remains (nirmālya).
Having worshipped the general *arghya*, one should offer it to the sun situated outside.
At the conclusion of the worship of Kula-Mārttaṇḍa, one should prepare a mandala with water;
using one's own hand, one who knows the proper measure should fashion the support for the worship.
In front, on the left side, upon one's own circular maṇḍala,
one should worship with the *praṇavas* and root mantras, using perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains. Then, having placed a conch vessel upon its base, one should fill it with water.
One should worship the jar, filled with the delight of the deity, once.
Having consecrated the water in the conch with a drop from that [jar] and a single *praṇava*,
one should worship it with the [mantras] beginning with *Śrī*, *Parā*, *Anākhyā*, *Saṃpat*, *Saubhāgya*, and *Jāti*.
One should sprinkle everything with those waters and then construct the mandala.
Having prepared the *yakṣakardama* paste from musk, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), fragrant substances, camphor, and saffron,
one should arrange it as an integral part of the worship.

On the ground smeared with that paste, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus in front. On its right side, one should draw two long squares; on its rear side, one should construct the Āgama-maṇḍala of the same measurement.
A square, a semicircle, a triangle, a hexagon, and a circle;
to its left, a long quadrangle for those who enjoy the *saṃvṛtta* and other [postures].
On that mandala, below [the deity], one should draw the mandala for the special arghya on one's own body:
a square, a circle, a hexagon, a circle, a triangle, and two crescents.
Within the lotus is the pleasing liṅga, and behind it is the divine scripture.
One should place [the deity] before the liṅga and draw the Saubhāgya-cakra.
One should extend the triangle, increasing it from the first-constructed yoni;
one should extend the primary yoni up to the limit of half the preceding triangle.
Likewise, one should extend the tip of the second womb by means of the previous triangle.
One should enclose this above with the line situated below the triangle.
[One should do so] from the upper line of the previous power, by piercing the sides of the outer angles.
Therefore, one should extend it downward, so that a fourth womb may arise.
One should extend the first womb from the middle triangle up to its apex.
From the apex of the first triangle, one should extend the triangle of the third womb downward.
One should likewise extend the upper line of the fourth triangle downward;
thus the fifth triangle is produced. Then, having pierced both sides of that [fifth triangle], one should extend them upward from the outer corner by means of a lower line.
One should extend [the lines] at the front of the side of the fourth womb toward the two first fronts;
having thus extended the square, [one proceeds] at the front of the side produced from the previous womb.
Having pierced the tips of the outer [triangles],
one should bind the two sides of the third triangle to the lower part of the first triangle; then,
one should extend the pair of tips from its sides to the tip of the fourth yoni, piercing it in all its positions.
Having drawn a large circle, one should draw a long six-petalled lotus;
outside of that, a sixteen-petalled lotus with four gates, preceded by the enclosure of the earth (dharāpura).
Having thus prepared the mandala and performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) as before, [one should proceed].
Having formed the *kamarīmudrā* with the seed-syllables (*bīja*) residing in the elements,
ending with the six [vowels] according to the divisions of the *Mātṛkā*, and with the *māyābīja* as before,
one should meditate upon the *Navātmā* in the heart through the yoga of dissolution and emanation.

Then, one should worship with the five jewels using mantras consisting of their respective seed-syllables enclosed by the *la* and *gha* vowels and the bindu, ending with the word "ratnam," along with the names of the realms known as Gaganam, Svargam, Martyam, and Pātālam.
Having worshipped Varuṇa, Indu, Yama, Indra, and the fifth [deity] in the intermediate directions,
one should worship Śrī-Parānākhyā once each within the [triangles of] Agni and the other directions, enclosed by the *tāra*. Then, one should sacrifice.

One should worship the deities once each within the middle triangle, the six-pointed star, and the [outer] triangles, according to their combined and individual classes, with wealth, good fortune, and knowledge. Having placed the vessel for worship upon its stand, one should fill it with the water of *arghya*.
Having cast the entire lotus and other [mandalas], one should perform the visualization of fire, sun, and moon;
likewise, through the processes of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, using white [syllables] as the root of creation.
One should contemplate the reversal of fortune, prosperity, and wealth through the seeds of good luck (*saubhāgyabīja*).
One should draw a hexagon joined with the syllables *ha*, *kṣa*, and *haṃsa*.
Then, having drawn a six-pointed star outside, one should worship it with jewels and pearls.
Having worshipped the venerable Parā three times through the processes of emanation and so forth in both direct and reverse order,
[one should offer] once and then thrice...
[with the rays] issuing from the two feet of the Moon and Sun situated at the *dvādaśānta*.

One should bring forth the *arghya*— filled with the great *kādyam*, produced from the fragments of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), and gathered from all intoxicating liquors. In this manner, for the sake of the great purpose, one should likewise invoke [the deities] separately by means of the two *vidyās*.
The Dhenu-yoni, the Mahā-yoni, the Triśikhā, and those resting upon the lotus;
by turning [the hands], one should make the two thumbs equal,
joining the two index fingers with the two middle fingers, and likewise the two little fingers with the two ring fingers.
Through mutual conjunction, this is proclaimed as the Yoni-mudrā.
Having crossed the two ring fingers in the añjali gesture, one should insert the two index fingers inside; with the two little fingers [also] inside, this is the Yoni-mudrā according to the teaching.
When the little fingers are tucked inside, this is called the Mahāyoni.
By joining the tips of the nails of the ring fingers with those of the index fingers while the palms are hollowed,
this is declared the Triśikhā mudrā, which arises from the open-palmed gesture.
One should apply [the mudrās] to the five nectars and display them. The little finger and the ring finger are joined together, back to back, with the middle fingers joined.
Joining the two thumbs face-to-face, one should extend the two index fingers like a staff;
this is the *saṃkṣobhaṇī* [mudrā], while by releasing the middle fingers it becomes the *drāviṇī*. In the *drāviṇī*, one should slowly bend the tips of the middle and index fingers inward.
The mudrā called Ākarṣiṇī has been described, and before that, the one known as Vaśyā. One should insert the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger into the hollow of one's own back;
with the palms, one should join the tips of the two index fingers to the tips of the thumbs in a secret manner.

One should slowly pull apart the two little fingers at their tips; having encircled them with the two middle fingers, and joining the tips of the middle fingers with the thumbs, one should extend the index fingers slightly apart—
this is the Unmādinī mudrā.
The contraction [of the fingers] directed toward her face is the Mahāṅkuśa mudrā; beyond that is the Khecarī.
Having formed the two hands in the shape of a rope, one places the yoni at the tip of the mudrā.
One should slowly join the two thumbs on the back of the little fingers;
the two middle fingers [are joined] on the back of the little fingers, and the two ring fingers on the backs of those [middle fingers].
This is the eighth seed-mudrā; the ninth is declared to be the *yoni*.
One should demonstrate affection and humility through various services and acts of attendance.
One should sprinkle everything with drops of *arghya* water, which are the rays of consciousness.
One should worship the three *śrīpādukās* upon the head and install the two triple-limbed (*tryaṅga*) mantras.
Having repeated [the mantra] three times in reverse order, one should perform the peace-offering (*śāntibali*) outside.
One should draw the four Vedas as the corners within the circle of the two oceans on the western side.
Having performed the sacrifice with the maṇḍala-mantra, one should place the bali offering upon its support.
It should consist of half-cooked rice, full of water, accompanied by its ingredients, and adorned with offered flowers.
With the casting of the mantra-eyes, one should partake in the threefold bali for peace.
Having offered a drop and brought [the deity] into the heart, one should worship the Great Mantra.
Having offered flowers three times... one should worship the flower three times.
Having meditated on the two feet within the aperture of the hand, and having reversed them, one should worship three times.
The rule for the offering of the seven services (*saptopacāra*) is not written here.
Having placed [the deity] within the heart, [and having placed] the feet [therein],
one should dissolve [it] into the heart.

Having worshipped Śrīparā and the Śrīguru at the crown of the head, and having performed worship at the sites of the *nyāsa* beginning with the five apertures, one should worship Śrīparā in the heart.
One should contemplate the two [deities] from the *liṅga* (the genitals) up to the *mūlādhāra*, ending at the trident.

Having fashioned the pedestal with the array of the thirty-six principles from the waking state up to the fourth state (turiya), one should worship it in three ways and invoke [the deity] three times through the process of emanation (sarga). Then,
one should consecrate it three times through the process of emanation, first by means of the [entire] emanation and then three times by means of the individual components of the pedestal.
Having performed the encapsulation (*sampuṭīkaraṇa*), one should worship with the *pūrṇā* offering three times.
Then, having recited the *śikhā-mantra* twenty-seven times,
and having worshipped with the *samanta-śikhā*, one should devoutly cast a handful of flowers.
Having worshipped [the deity] three times in the heart, one should unite one's own self with it;
having worshipped the venerable Supreme Consciousness, one should commence the Mahārthakrama.
Having worshipped the venerable Guru, who is the essence of Bhaṭṭa-Bhaṭṭāraka, upon the head,

one should worship the four seats (pīṭhas) on the crown, at the base of the navel, and in the mouth. Furthermore, the pair of seed-syllables for Māyā and Lakṣmī should be placed at the beginning of all mantras.
One should proclaim the circle of Yoginīs according to the secret and manifest doctrine.
At the end of each mantra, one should employ the formula: "I worship the Pādukā.
Then [one worships] Padmāsanā, then Siṃhāsanā, and then Pretāsanā.
One should worship [the goddesses] beginning from the right ear and ending at the left on the forehead,
as proclaimed in the venerable Mahānaya-āgama according to the sequence of the five vehicles:
Khecarī, Gocarī, and then Dikcarī.
One should join the word "Vyomavāmeśvarī Ambā" to the five [names].
After Kramagaṇapati-nātha, one should likewise add his beloved Ambikā; similarly, after Kramapaṭuka, his beloved Ambā is proclaimed.
Then one should worship the group of six— namely, the Lord (*nātha*), Kuleśvarī, and Parāmbikā— above the location of the five currents (*pañcavāha*).
One should then worship the three lines situated at the head and the three seats (*pīṭha*).
First Kaulagiri, then [the others]...;
ending with Dakāpīṭha, these are situated on the seat of the lineage (pāramparyāsana).
Bimbādevī, Rāmā, Mūradevī, and the others—these phonemes are near to the Goddess Ambikā.
The Goddess [is present] through the triad in the divine stream...
the innate [nature], the auspicious musical instrument, and the primordial one.
Nārāyaṇa and Kumāra—these are one [deity].
Then one should worship the fourfold group consisting of the Pīṭha, the Pīṭheśa, and the Pīṭheśī.
Oḍyāṇa-pīṭha is located in the two ankles; its Lord is on the right shoulder.
Her sovereign lady is on the back of the ear; likewise, there is a triad known as Vāmā.
Pūrṇādi-pīṭha, Pūrṇeśa, and Pūrṇāmbā are proclaimed;
likewise, there is a triad beginning with Kāmākṣī.
Likewise, in the root, the heart, and the bindu, as well as in the center of the spinal column and so forth,
are Jālandharapīṭha, Jāleśa, and likewise Jālāmukhī at the tip.
These twelve rays are indicated in the Mahārthaśāsana.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) at the appropriate locations with the mantras known as the *anuviloma*.
According to one's capacity, one should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) of the *bindu* in the heart by means of the *anākhyā* mantra.
Likewise, one should perform this with the *saptapiṇḍa* mantra and touch [the body] down to the secret parts.
One should bring a vessel containing the three oblations (balitraya) along with its base;
having placed it on one's right side, one should cast a flower together with the *bindu*.
One should then recite the three mantras known as *anu*, *śakti*, and *śivā*.
Having formed the nārāca-mudrā and gazing with a piercing look,
one should clench the two hands into fists and extend the two index fingers like staffs.
One should slowly draw the left hand forward and then the right hand backward;
this is declared to be the Nārāca-mudrā, which is to be employed when offering the bali-oblation.
It is addressed as "O Vaṭukanātha," followed by "O Son of the Goddess."
At the end of *kapilā*, at the end of *jaṭābhārabhāsurā*, one should utter *triṇetraka*.
At the end of *jvālā*, one should likewise utter *avatarayugala*. Then [one should say]: "O beloved of Agni, accept this offering (*bali*), accept this worship (*pūjā*)."
Then, having uttered the word "sarva" (all), followed by the word "yoginībhyaḥ" (to the Yoginīs),
and then the words for "khecarībhyo gocarībhyo dikcarībhyaḥ" (to those who move in the sky, those who move on the earth, and those who move in the quarters),
and also the words for "bhūcarībhyastrailokyānte nivāsinībhyaḥ" (to those who move on the ground and those dwelling at the end of the three worlds).
"O beloved of Agni, accept this offering and this worship!
Whatever Yoginīs there may be— whether fierce or gentle,
terrible or even more terrible— and also the two imperishable [syllables] 'pa' and 'ca'."

May all those who move through the sky (khecarīs), those who move on the earth (gocarīs), as well as those who move in the cardinal directions (dikcarīs) and those who move upon the ground (bhūcarīs), be satisfied by this rite of offering (balikarma). May those established in the seat honored by heroes— known as the Ground of Peace (śāntibhūmi)— attain firm stability.

At the place of Kṣāṃ, one should offer this oblation and worship to Kṣetrapāla with the mantra: "Kṣetreśvara, accept, accept," ending with the wife of Agni (Svāhā). One should then display the mudrās known as the three claps (tālatraya) and the staff (daṇḍa) for the field.
Having offered the stream of drops at the end, one should worship the [deities] beginning with Sṛṣṭi as before.
Having honored the full vessel along with its side-dish on the right of the *arghya* water—

One should worship Pūrṇeśī with the *upadaṃśa* (side-dish) according to the method to be described hereafter. One should consecrate it with a drop from the vessel used for worship and offer it to the venerable Guru, together with the concluding *pūrṇāhuti*, along with the accompanying verses.
One should joyfully remember the three principles and the root-vidyā simultaneously;
having accepted and touched the self, one should purify those who have already been purified.
Thereafter, one should commence the worship of the Goddess Śrīsampadīśvarī.
Having placed the auspicious Kāmayantra seat in the center of the previously described area at the base,
and having worshipped it once, one should install Sṛṣṭikāmeśvarī. Then,
having served her with that mantra, one should worship her three times with the mantra.
Then, at the end of the *Sundarī* mantra— consisting of the seed-syllable, *Śiva*, and *Kāma*— one should place the *Hṛdaya* (Heart) mantra.
Having thus placed the *Vākcakra* (Speech Wheel) in the heart, with its pericarp named *Kāmayantra*,
one should install *Haṃsa* as its seat and worship it once, as before.
Having established that state upon its seat, one should worship it threefold with the ritual offerings.
One should lead [the deity] into the union by means of the mantras beginning with *tad-bīja*, *Śiva*, and *Kāma*.
This is the great lotus of the Mothers (*mātṛ*), whose form is the pericarp of the wheel of speech.
Having recollected that seat and performed the *haṃsa*-nyāsa, one should worship it once.
Having placed the dissolution (*saṃhṛti*) upon its lap, one should worship it thrice with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*).
One should lead [the deity] into the womb by means of the mantras beginning with the seed-syllable of Śiva and Kāma. [The goddess] seated within the lotus-casket.
Having meditated upon the succession of scriptures and performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the *mātṛkā* as before,
one should perform the arrangement of the fingers in the gesture of the swan (*haṃsa*) and worship with the *haṃsa* mantra.
From the end [of the mantra], one offers to Sadāśiva Mahāpreta Padmāsana at the heart. Then, one should invoke the Goddess seated upon that throne with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*).
One should worship the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and the garland (*mālā*) with the root mantra.
Having worshipped the limbs of repose and enjoyment, as well as the Mistress of the seventy million [mantras],
one should worship Rati, Prīti, and Manobhavā within the triangle at the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
preceded by the seed-syllables of Speech, Power, and Desire.
The Brāhmī Mālā begins with the syllable *ī*; Śivā begins with *ī*.
Ūhā begins with *ī* as Kaumārī; by the mind (*manas*), Vaiṣṇavī begins with *ī*.
Āṣā begins with *ī* as Vārāhī; Aiśā begins with *ī*... [and so forth].
One should worship Pūrvacaṇḍikā [in the center].
Outside, one should worship the eight short vowels beginning with 'a' joined with the eight consonants from 'kṣa' to 'la'.
One should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Asita as before in the second enclosure.
With Indra, Agni, Yama, and Rakṣas, [and the others],
one should worship Vaṭuka, Gaṇapa, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla together with their seed-syllables (*bīja*),
using the *kalā*-mantras proclaimed in the Āgamas.
[Having performed] the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*...
[one] should begin the sequence of... (p. 36).

First, one should unite oneself [with the deity], and thereafter, the Cakrāsana. The mantra ending with "to the Cakrāsana"— namely, *rendu-kāma-ra-śukla-śūla-visargakaḥ cakrāsanāya*— is situated upon the Cakrāsana.

One should fix the heart [mantra] for the sake of the seat of the accomplishment of the goal, joined with the powers of *māyā* and *kāma*. One should perform the worship of the seats for both the mantras and the deities.
One should recite the Vāgbhava mantra, consisting of five peaks— space, moon, fire,
earth, and moon—
and the Śākta vidyā (for the rite of invoking the Goddess), with the [syllables] ending in fire and the internal emission.
Having crossed the palms with the two index fingers interlaced,
this is the Trikhaṇḍā mudrā for invocation; through its union with the Vidyā-mudrā,
one raises the Kuṇḍalinī power.
Having drawn forth the goddess Tripurasundarī who resides in the center of the wheel and established her through the yoga of meditation, one should bring her face-to-face with oneself;
and by means of the primary and secondary offerings, one should perform the worship of the limbs of dissolution.
And having visualized the interior of the sky as the single line of the Great Triangle (mahātryaśra),
the fifteen Nityās are proclaimed in sequence, beginning with the first lunar day (pratipad) and ending with the full moon (paurṇamāsī): from Kāmeśvarī up to Citrā.
Then [there are] Kāmeśvarī Nityā, Bhagamālinī Nityā, as well as Nityaklinnā, Bheruṇḍā, and Vahnivāsinī.
Mahāvidyeśvarī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, Kulasundarī,
Nityā, Nīlapatākā, Vijayā, Sarvamaṅgalā,
Jvālāmālinī, Citrā, and Mahātripurasundarī.
From Citrā to Kāmeśvarī, worshipped in reverse order during the dark fortnight;

first, one should worship Mahātripurasundarī in the center at the time of the *visarga*. One should then apply the respective *nityā* goddesses, who embody their specific lunar days, to those situated in the middle.
One should enclose [the mantra] with the *ṣoḍaśī* (the sixteen vowels) three times each through the method of worship.
Then, one should worship the fifteen [vowels] in their respective sounds in direct order (*ānuloma*).
Furthermore, the pair of seed-syllables for Māyā and Lakṣmī should be placed at the beginning of all mantras.

At the end of the mantra, one should insert the name followed by "nityā śrīpādukāṃ pūjayāmy ataḥ" (I worship the eternal, glorious pādukā). Alternatively, that which begins with the seed-syllables of Kāma and Śakti, ends with the letter Sa, and is accompanied by the Bindu— namely, "kāmeśvarī-cchā-kāme"— bestows the fruit.
Thereafter, one should employ the *pada* that brings all sentient beings under control as before.
One should utter: "O you who cause the agitation of the world! Hrūṃ hrūṃ drāṃ drīṃ klīṃ klīṃ!"
One should utter the seed-syllables *blūṃ* and *saḥ* in reverse order.
Thus is the mantra of Kāmeśvarī; after that follows Bhagamālinī.
At the end of the seed-syllable of Speech (*vāgbīja*), one should utter *bhaga-bhage bhagini*.
Likewise, at the end of "Bhagodarī," one should utter "bhaga" at the conclusion;
[namely: "O you who bring forth the bhaga, O you whose secret is the bhaga, O you whose womb is the bhaga, O you who strike down with the bhaga!"

* * * * * * * * * * * * । * * in the form of the eternally moist vulva (*bhaga*), one should then utter the word "vulva" (*bhaga*). In the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), [one should utter] "all my vulvas" (*sarvabhagāni mehyān*) and then the words.
"O Giver of Boons, O Wondrous One, O Pure One, O You whose limbs are moistened;
O You who are dripping with moisture, cause [them] to be moistened...
cause [them] to be agitated and agitate."
One should utter the words "sarvasattvān," followed by the word "bhageśvarī," and then recite: "vāgbhūṃ ca bhūṃ ca ṣeṃ bhūṃ ca moṃ bhūṃ he bhūṃ.
Then one should say: "O Vāgklinne, [purify] all my vulvae (bhaga) and my words (pada)."

At the end, one should utter "bring her under control" (*vaśamānaya ca*) and "seize the woman" (*strīṃ hara*). Having extracted the mantra ending with the seed-syllable of *māyā* (Hrīṃ), one should recite the *Gagamālinī*:
"O you who are joined with *māyā* and *nityā*, O *klinne*, O you whose essence is the flow of intoxication, O beloved of Fire! (*māyānityayutaklinne madadravegnivallabhā*).
"Nityaklinna" is thus proclaimed, and Bheruṇḍā follows thereafter.
After that is the goad (aṅkuśa) preceded by the Vedas (the syllable *oṃ*), followed by the pair of seed-syllables *bhroṃ* and *kroṃ*.
Then *dhrauṃ*, *jrauṃ*, and *chrauṃ*, ending with the wife of fire (*svāhā*); at the end of that is Vahnivāsinī.

One should utter "Dhruvam Māyām Vahnivāsinyai Namaḥ. Then, having said "Dhruvante Pheṃ Saḥ," followed by "Nityaklinne Madadrave," ending with the wife of Fire (Svāhā), this is declared to be the mantra of Mahāvidyeśvarī.
The mantra of Hṛddūtī is declared as *dhruvaṃ māyā śivādūtyai*.
Then follows *dhruvaṃ māyāṃ tathā huṃ khe ca che kṣastrīṃ*, and after that, the supreme [mantra].

"Huṃ kṣeṃ hrīṃ phaṭ" is proclaimed as the mantra of Tvaritā Parameśvarī. The seed-syllables of Vāk, Kāma, and Śakti belong to Śrībālā and Kulasundarī. With these five arrows—drāṃ, drīṃ, klīṃ, blūṃ, and saḥ—the Nityās are invoked.
One should utter "māyā phreṃ srūṃ krom āṃ kāmavāk blū.
At the end of "nityā," joined with "mada," [one says] "drave huṃ phreṃ.
[This] is red, known as Nīlapatākā, and ends with the seed-syllable of Māyā.
Then, O Lord of the Arghya, [the mantra] consisting of the bee, the trident, and the bindu-piṇḍa is called Vijayā;
she is Saumitī, the eternal Nityā, the All-Auspicious One (Sarvamaṅgalā).
[The mantra] beginning with *dhruvam*, followed by *hṛd* and ending with *bhagavati*, [and then] *jāla*... [is the mantra].

And at the end of the withdrawal of the elements (*bhūtasaṃhāra*), having uttered the two *kārikās* and "in the fire-born one" (*jātavedasi*), [one recites] the pair of blazing mantras: "blaze, blaze!
(*prajvala prajvala*). Then, having uttered the pair of *māyā-marma* weapons:
Ending with the wife of Vahni (the letter *ra*), she is proclaimed as [the goddess];
the fifteenth digit, Citrā, is proclaimed by the people as beginning with the root-seed (*mūlabīja*). Thus is Tripurasundarī Nityā described.
Having worshipped the sixteen eternal [energies], one should contemplate them as encapsulated by their own respective vowels.
Then, beginning from the subterranean chamber (*bhūgṛha*), one should worship the nine enclosures (*navāvaraṇa*).
...the final [powers] of those mixed with the others:
after that, *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, and *mahimā* are designated as belonging to Śiva.
The desire for the enjoyment of sovereign power (*prākāmya*) follows immediately after being attached to mastery (*vaśitva*).
That which is known as attainment (*prāpti*) resides in the southern of the four gates of all desires;
[the others reside] in the left and so forth... [omitted].
One should worship [the goddesses] in the eight directions beginning with the left side.
In the ninefold worship (navāvaraṇa-pūjā), the commencement is before the principal deity;
the Sovereigns of the Wheels (cakreśvarīs), beginning with the Root-Vidyā and ending with the Goddess, are worshipped in the sequence of nine.
Tripurā, Tripureśī, Sundarī, Puravāsinī,
and Tripurasundarī—
there one should worship the Mistress of the Cakras (Cakreśvarī) by means of the worship of each respective cakra.
During the worship, one should display the mudrās for each cakra in sequence:
Saṃkṣobha, Drāvaṇa, Ākarṣa, Vaśya, Unmāda, Mahāṅkuśa, Khecarī, Bīja, and the one called Yoni; these are declared to be the nine mudrās.
The traditions are thus protected, even more protected, and supreme;
they are those that have transcended the Kula, the innermost essence, and the great secrets.
They abide in the secret of the higher and the lower, and possess the secret preceded by delight.
In the nine wheels, the Yoginīs reside individually under their respective names.
41) The wheel that fascinates the three worlds fulfills all desires.
The wheel that agitates all, the bestower of all good fortune;
the wheel that accomplishes all aims, as well as that which provides all protection;
the wheel that removes all diseases, known as the bestower of all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
Having first understood the ninefold central [deity] consisting of all bliss as the lord of the wheel, one should worship the fourfold conventions:
the leading goddesses, the nine mudrās, the yoginīs, and the lords of the wheels.
Having worshipped the heroine Tripurā, one should display the mudrā with the seed-syllable (bīja).
The mudrā is Saṃkṣobhaṇī; the offering is made by means of the remaining two conventions. These are the manifest Yoginīs in the Trailokyamohana [cakra].
He performed worship with all the ritual offerings, saying in due order, "May they be honored.
In the second enclosure, there are sixteen mantras preceded by the vowels;
these are the Nityās, the Kalās, each situated at the end of a separate mantra.

One should employ the sixteen mantras ending with *ātman*, *amṛta*, and *śarīra*: namely, *kāma-buddhi*, *ahaṃkāra*, *śabda*, *sparśa*, *rūpa*, *rasa*, *gandha*, *citta*, *dhairya*, *smṛti*, *nāma*, *sabhīja*, *ātman*, *amṛta*, and *śarīra*.
Thereafter, one should worship Cakreśvarī and Tripureśvarī with the two vidyās. Then, having formed the Drāviṇī mudrā with the syllable *drīṃ*, one should display it.
These are the Guptayoginīs, who fulfill all desires.
One should say, "May they be worshipped with all ritual services," and worship the second enclosure in a counter-clockwise direction.
* * * * * * revolving in the sky upon the eight petals of the directions: Anaṅgakusumā in the east, Anaṅgamekhalā in the south,
Anaṅgamadanā in the west, and Madanāturā in the north.
In the northwest, one should worship Īśāna, Anaṅgamālinī,
the Mistress endowed with Vidyā, and Tripurasundarī.
Having displayed the *karṣiṇī* mudrā (the "attraction" gesture), one should utter their mantra.
One should say: "May those Yoginīs of the Saguptaka [mandala], known as Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and the rest, be pleased, having been worshipped with all ritual offerings in the circle.
One should worship the fourth enclosure within, proceeding counter-clockwise.
The fourteen [powers] are proclaimed, beginning with Sarvā and ending with Śakti:
Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī-śakti, likewise Sarvavidrāvinī,
Sarvākarṣaṇa-śakti, and Sarvāplāvanakāriṇī.
The deluder, the paralyzer, the stupifier, and the subjugator;
the one with rays, the exhilarator, and likewise the accomplisher of all aims;
the fulfiller of prosperity, consisting of mantra, and the destroyer of dualities.
One should utter the words: "Śrīcakranāyikā, endowed with the Vidyā, Tripurasundarī;
Vāsinī joined with the seed-syllable *blūṃ*, [and] the mudrā called Vaśyā—these are the Yoginīs of the tradition, bestowers of all prosperity."
One should say, "May they be pleased, having been worshipped with all ritual services," and then worship the ten goddesses of the fifth enclosure on the left.
One should worship [the goddesses] beginning with Sarvā and ending with Ādidevī on the two sets of ten spokes;
she is the bestower of all accomplishments, the bestower of prosperity, the one who makes all dear,
the one who brings about auspiciousness at the end, and likewise the bestower of all desires.
She is the liberator from suffering and the pacifier of death and its precursors; thereafter, she is the remover of obstacles, beautiful in all her limbs,
the bestower of good fortune, the primordial Vidyā, and the Mistress of the Cakra.
"O Śrīśa, [protect] Tripurā," and so forth; this is the Mudrā known as Unmādasamśrikā.
These are the Yoginīs of Kulakaula; therefore, for the accomplishment of all aims, one should utter:
"May they be worshipped."
The sixth enclosure is in the inner ten-spoked wheel, arranged counter-clockwise:
[the goddesses] Sarvajñā, Sarvaśakti, and likewise Sarvaiśvaryapradā;
then Sarvajñānamayī, and finally Sarvavyādhivināśinī.
Subsequently, she consists of all bliss and has the nature of all protection;
at the end, one should worship her in the ten-spoked [cakra], for she bestows the fruit of all desires.
United with the Vidyā, she is the Mistress of the Cakra (Cakranāthā), known as Tripuramālinī.
"O Yoginīs, who are the makers of all protection! Likewise, one should say:
'May you, who have been worshipped with all ritual offerings in the circle, be pleased.'"
One should worship the group of eight beginning with Vaśinī in an anti-clockwise direction in the [cardinal] directions.
[One should perform] the Khecarī mudrā accompanied by its seed-syllable. These... [and so forth].

One should utter the words "may they be worshipped," and then worship the four weapons known as the Kāma-bāṇa, Āsa, Śāpa, and Kuśa-heti in the two intermediate spaces on the sides of the central triangle.
"Salutation to the eternal seed-syllables, to the Jambhanas, and to the Bāṇas"; "Salutation to Dharma... [and so forth] ... for the sake of battle, salutation to the Pāśa."
One should utter "Kroṃ, salutation to the goad for immobilization" up to that point.
Then, one should worship [the deities] in the center, at the tip, on the right, on the left, and in the middle of the central triangle.
Alternatively, thereafter, one should perform the worship of the seed-syllables of Kāma and Śakti, both individually and collectively.
Kāmeśvarī... [and so forth] ...
likewise Bhagnamālā on the left; in the center is Tripurasundarī.
Beyond the other wheels beginning with the Mūlavidyā is Tripurāmbā, who is supreme.
And having joined [the hands] connected to that, one should perform the two mudrās born of the seed-syllables and the womb-syllable, namely Hraum and Aimit, for Mahātripurasundarī.

These deities, having extracted the [respective] words, reside in the secret [center], which bestows all accomplishments. Likewise, they reside in the wheel consisting of universal bliss and provided with all ritual offerings.
One should say, "May they be worshipped," and thus the ninth enclosure (āvaraṇa) is described. At the end of that, one should offer a handful of flowers with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā).
Then, one should display the nine mudrās, each conjoined with its respective seed-syllable (bīja).
One should demonstrate affection and reverence through various services and offerings. By means of the yoga of internalizing the nectar within the vessel of enjoyment,
and having contemplated the identity of oneself with the deity, one should begin the worship according to the Śāmbhava method.
One should unite the Gatekeepers and the rest with the Mistress of the Family (Kuleśī) according to the sequence of the enclosures.
One should utter the mantra "niśāṭanāya," encapsulated by the seed-syllable *hrauṃ*.
Between the two *hrauṃ* seed-syllables, one should pronounce "tameraya."
One should join [the seed-syllables] *hakṣaum* at the beginning and end with *kālānalāya reta*.
Thus, with these three mantras, one should first worship the triad of fiery forms (*tejomūrtti*) located in the throat,
the heart, and the mouth, for the purpose of invoking the deity.
Standing in the right, left, and middle [positions], they do not [resemble] corpses, dogs, or rams;
they resemble white, blood-red, and yellow [colors], bearing tridents, swords, mallets, and the gesture of threat,
while being very serene, three-eyed, and beautifully adorned.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the vapas and then worship the mantra-pīṭhas,
according to the divisions of the southern water, the northern water, and the middle region.
At the end of the Vāṅ-mantra and the deity-mantra, and likewise for the fivefold *praṇava*,

one should first recite the five mantras and then meditate upon their fivefold forms. These are the five deities, appearing respectively as red and white in their various parts, and resembling beautiful women and men.

One should meditate upon the couple in the central lotus, surrounded by the five forms; they have three eyes, are reeling with intoxication, are adorned with all ornaments, and their hands hold a mudrā, a book, a rosary, and a water-pot, with the Praṇava (Om) at the tip of their noses.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who is seated upon the body of the God, adorned with the aforementioned marks,
enriched by the instruction of the supreme reality, and situated on all sides within the five forms,
one should worship her according to the scripture with the single Vidyā.
Then, the worship of the five gurus is performed starting from the center and moving to the left;
[proceeding] right, left, right, left, and back to the center...
[one should worship] the leaders, who consist of two pairs of kalpas and vedas.
To the Gurus, the Nathas, and the primordial ones, the inconceivable friends who are the Lords of Kula;
[to them] together with their respective Mothers, whose names end in their own initial seed-syllables;
[and to those who] bestow supreme fearlessness...
First, you should worship me, and afterwards the gurus; then follows the worship of the seats (*pīṭha*).

One should meditate upon the seat of the corpse (*pretāsana*) in the center of the pericarp of the great lotus—reddish in color, with its head lying supine, and possessing two hands as fire and power (*śakti*).
Then, one should worship it three times with the second *tāra* mantra.
One should then visualize a great lotus arisen from its navel.
One should worship the hexagon within the pericarp of that [lotus] three times with the *vāgbhava* syllable.
Having thus worshipped the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should perform the special three-limbed rite.
Then, having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the "breaking of the staff" (*daṇḍabhaṅgi*), one should perform the three-limbed rite for the deity.
Then, having performed the placement of the three limbs of the Goddess, one should perform the placement of the *piṇḍas*.
Having placed the seed-syllables, the sixteen-fold pervasive [placement], and the mantras, one should recite them in the heart.
Then, one should worship the Heart [of the deity] three times with the mantras of the God of Gods and the Goddess.
One should examine the movement of the breath—whether it flows through the left, the right, or equally through both.
When it is in the left, it is the Moon; when in the right, it is Day; and when equal, it is the Fire-maṇḍala.
That radiance, known as the seat of the ears, arises from the differentiation of these three maṇḍalas.
From the root, one should raise the *kuṇḍalinī*—the seed of the vital points—with the goad;
through the channel of the *suṣumnā*, [one reaches] the lunar orb of consciousness at the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
[One should contemplate it] as nourished by the nectar of the innate state of aesthetic flavor (*sāmarasya*).
One should bring the *prabaha* [vital breath] into the channel through the conjunction of touch at that specific time.
Having drawn that radiance (*tejas*) outwards, one should place it within the lotus of the deceased (*pretapadma*).
Then, one should meditate upon the God and the Goddess by means of the path previously described.
One should offer the ten services (daśopacāra) at intervals between the two root mantras.
One should worship with water, a mirror, a conch, a bell, and a fly-whisk;
and one should offer dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, unbroken rice grains, garlands, and fruits.
Having visualized the *suka* three times at the crown of the head, one should perform the *yonimudrā* three times;
immediately thereafter, one should clearly manifest each individual syllable of the root mantra.
Holding [these] individually:
first, the Brahma-hand, followed by those known as the trident and the discus, the banner, and the two boon-granting hands; this is declared to be the sixfold Brahma-foot.
The one named Pāribhadraprasūna, the rosary for recitation (jāpyamālā),
the book, Abhaya, and Daśamoheti— these are considered to be four separate [deities] ending in the dative case.
These deities, expanded and magnified, are to be worshipped at the front of the arms of the [principal] form.
The eight [syllables] beginning with Maṅgala are conjoined with the eight beginning with Brāhmī.
