Arghīśa, joined with the Bindu, is the Lord situated within the eight seed-syllables.
One should utter Sūkṣmā, joined with the Bindu, within the seed-syllables.
One should join the word "Mahābhairava" separately at the end of each name:
Maṅgala, Carcaka, Yoga, Harasiddha, Bhaṭṭaka,
followed by Kilikila, Kālarātri, and the one known as Bhīṣaṇa.
Meditation has been previously described for these [mantras] which illuminate the Lord of Rays (Raśminātha).
One should join them with the heart in the auspicious Śāmbhava [tradition], within the Saubhāgya of the venerable Parā.
Having worshipped the limbs of the dissolution and enjoyment of the two deities, one should recite [the mantra] a hundred times;
then, with the root mantras being honored, one should bring [them], along with their limbs, to dissolution within the heart. [One should place them] upon the head... [etc.]
To Him whose nature is born from the power of Vaikuṇṭha;
who dwells within the Bindu at the navel of the supporting Sādhi; |||
Salutations to Him whose body moves through the final course of the sixteen digits of the moon,
who [destroys] the suffering of birth, worldly enjoyment, dissolution, and disease,
and who brings about the destruction of the very existence of [dualistic] being.

O Lord of Men, for the sake of attaining both worldly enjoyment and liberation, one should daily recite this purifying hymn consisting of five verses, which is the singular form that destroys wrinkles and graying hair.
She who moves by means of the Vedas, the words, the meters, the oceans, and the swift winds;
she who performs her strides upon the earth by means of the Vedas and the words—
she is manifest [as the Goddess].
I bow to Him whose light illumines the world, which consists of the nature of the knower,
the knowable, and the means of knowledge, and which is the state of emanation resting within Him.

This very Self, whose intention is that of the authoritative one, shines forth as the non-dual, having cast aside all distinctions; I am that unsurpassed abode. While the Supreme Space flows as a single unity, the four [directions] proceed within it.
...by means of the body of the manifold variety of internal and external sense objects, whose nature is Śiva. (p. 50)
Victorious is Paraśiva, the Lord of these five rivers:
she who consists of desire, skin, poetry, and bliss; she who is the creative power (*kalā*) of Śambhu, the God of Desire; she whose delight is the play of coming and going.

May the blessed Sarasvatī— who shines within those whose minds are disciplined by the realization "I am [She]," who has embraced all consciousness and its objects, and who bestows prosperity— be for your delight.
She resembles the rising sun, with the crescent moon of youth shining upon her crest.

I remember Vāṇī, who has three eyes and who causes supreme fear to her enemies. I bow to the Supreme Śiva, who is marked by the five acts (kṛtyas) and whose nature is the perfect I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) through his non-difference from the entire universe.

I bow to that one Great Being, the eye of all, to whom the threefold reality is divided according to the sequence of the praiser, the praised, and the act of praise. I remember that supreme Speech, which rests upon the sequence beginning with Paśyantī.
She who possesses the form of great majesty, manifesting in the appearance of various tastes;
she who shines in whatever form— whether as place, time, or object— according to each respective thing, yet without depending upon consciousness or its parts.

I worship that body of Mahātripurasundarī, which destroys worldly existence, which shines like lightning, and extends from the root-center (mūlādhāra) to the crown of the head (bilapa). [She who is] like a golden flower in the womb (yonimudrā) and radiant as a flash of lightning in the heart.
In worship, O Maheśvarī, your great splendor is like the moon;
it satiates all things moving and unmoving with a flood of spreading nectar-rays.
O Bhavānī, for the sake of the pacification of worldly existence, I meditate upon you, the immortal Mistress (Amṛteśvarī).
O Goddess of gods, color, digit, mantra, principle, word, and even the world— thus the group of six above shines within you, whose self is consciousness.
O Mother, you unfold this wondrous and marvelous diversity, beginning from Anāśrita and ending with Kālāgnirudra; for within you, whose very body is light, O Goddess,
all that shines forth consisting of name, form, and action.
All that does not exceed you, whose very body is light.
At the edge of the network of the eyes and other senses, through the play of the lotus-throne of the heart,
O Goddess, you enjoy the honey of form and the rest, which is beyond all comparison.

Having fully pervaded the sense-objects with the nectar of immortality, the goddesses of consciousness always send them for the sake of the yogis and indeed for the purpose of your worship. This secret Heart of Good Fortune was [revealed] by the yogi Śivānanda.
This *Tripurā-stotra*, which grants all desires when remembered for the sake of perfecting one's propitiation, has thus been composed;
it reveals the supreme truth and is honored by the best of yogis.
Let those endowed with devotion practice the ritual of worship, which has no purpose other than the destruction of all sins and sufferings;
[let them offer] the flower of hymns, which is worthy of being honored by the circle of rays of consciousness.
I investigate the great worship; for such discernment is indeed extremely rare.
O you whose nature is the multitude [of deities]!
Obeisance to you who are perfected in your full-fledged form, O Tripurasundarī!
O slow-moving one with a wondrous body ranging from Kāmeśvarī to Citrā;
O Great Goddess, O highly fortunate one, obeisance to you... [repeated].
O Purasundarī!
O Ocean of Consciousness, who art the support of all! Homage to you, Tripurasundarī, whose form is constituted of the six limbs within the six powers beginning with omniscience.
O Earth that gives birth to the jewels of the great siddhis such as *aṇimā*, O Goddess whose splendor is the unfolding and closing of the universe! Homage to you, O Tripurasundarī!
O eternal moonlight of the full moon of consciousness, which is the essence of the digits of knowledge!
Obeisance to you, O Tripurasundarī, who have extinguished the net of the world;
obeisance to you, O Tripurasundarī, who are garlanded by the rising rays of Anaṅgakusumā and the other [Śaktis].
Obeisance to you, O Tripurasundarī, who have spread out the multitude of worlds.
Salutations, O Tripurasundarī, whose every limb is perfumed by the garlands of great consciousness beginning with Kṣobhiṇī;
you who abide in the channels of prāṇa and apāna, and who are beyond the reach of Viṣṇu and Śiva.
O Mahāmāyā, O Mahābindu, salutations to you, O Tripurasundarī! You who abide in the entire path, who are dear to the heart, whose essence is the digits of Kāmarāja;
O you whose form consists of Bindu, Nāda, and Kalā, salutations to you, O Tripurasundarī!
This unprecedented and unfading flower of a hymn unfolds, blossoming with the nectar of Śiva’s bliss and nourished by the fragrance of intuitive insight.
[It honors] her of the crimson limbs, the most beloved of Śiva, the God of Love, whose lotus-feet are slightly reddened.
I bow to the auspicious Goddess, whose creeper-like body is adorned with radiant jewels, who possesses a pair of eyes,
and whose left hand holds a shimmering skull-cup filled with honey-liquor;
her other raised hand holds a ladle that is no larger than the former, and she bestows all prosperity.
Thus one should recite the hymn with devotion and cast a flower with palms joined in prayer.
Regarding the recitation of the hymn, there is no fixed rule for devotees due to the power of their spiritual fitness;
in matters of degree—whether little or much—one does not incur any fault by exceeding [the prescribed amount].
An improper hymn was recited by someone due to an excess [of syllables].
Outside the great lotus, in the four corners of the earthen chamber:

[and] the Guru’s feet and Kulāmbikā enclosed by the seed-syllable *māyā* (*śrauṃ*).
One should perform the external worship with [mantras] ending in the dative case, each having a separate origin.
Having touched me, one should worship with a single vidyā.
Having worshipped three times, the Marīcis are in the six corners beginning with the forehead.
Having worshipped [the deity] as in the morning recollection, one should lead [the consciousness] into dissolution within the *svādhiṣṭhāna*.
Having worshipped the two deities there, [one perceives] rays of light in the six *ādhāras*.
The bases are established...
[the circles] have the form of fire-petals and taste-petals;
they possess circular sounds, and their colors are like the sun—turbid with the time of the leaf-fall and yet pure white.

To the west of the Prācīna-śānti-bali, having prepared two mandalas—

There should be two vessels, one half-filled with food and the other full, both marked with the saṃbindu.
One should consecrate the offering for the Saubhāgyavidyā with the *śānti* mantra;
one should present the offering in the Śāmbhava [mandala] with the mantra known as Kṣetrapāla.
[This is done] with the syllables *tāra*, *māyā*, *vyoma*, *varma*, *bindu*, *saṃvarta*, and *bindu*.
Above the word *jvālāmukha*, one should join [the rest] by the command of Bhairava:
*māṃsāvṛto rakṣa rakṣa hrūṃ svāhā*.
This twenty-four-syllable mantra belongs here to Kṣetreśa in the Śāmbhava [tradition].
When this has been accomplished, everything becomes easily achieved; of this there is no doubt.
Having displayed the mudrā, one should cause the stream of drops from the arghya to dissolve into the heart.

The three door-keepers and the serpent-germs (āgamāṇus) are in the eyes; likewise, the dissolution of Saṃvarta and the other gurus occurs in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmabila). And the dissolution of the ten weapons and their bodies occurs at the tips of their respective arms.

Having brought about the dissolution of the eight couples beginning with Maṅgala, along with their limbs and the lords of the Gaṇas, and having led the dissolution of the God and Goddess [into the Self], one should dissolve those two into the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*).
One should lead the sequential stages residing in the body to dissolution therein;
and one should offer oneself in the worship of the venerable supreme consciousness (*śrīparā-saṃvit*).
Thus has been described the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*), which is one's own identity with the Great Purpose (*mahārtha*), and not otherwise.
In the worship of the consciousness of Śrī-Sampat, through the worship of the partless (niṣkala), there is dissolution.
Having perceived the partless consciousness of the Kāmakalā within the central abode of the deities situated in the wheel of the nine enclosures (āvaraṇas), one should contemplate it.

Having visualized the *bindu* as the face, one should contemplate the two breasts beneath it; below that, the lower half [of the triangle], facing downwards. Having thus meditated upon the *Kāmakalā* and having formed the *khecarī-mudrā*:

One should perform the worship of the Kula-Ācāṇḍa at the conclusion of the offering-vessel.
One should worship the Lotus there, which has turned away from the Vedas; one should meditate upon it as having three bends and three fruits,
with three folds below the center, resting upon a circular pedestal.
His waist and upper body are gracefully poised, he is dark-complexioned, and his limbs are fully developed.
He holds a sword in his right hand and a blue lotus in his left,
and is adorned with jeweled necklaces, bracelets, armlets, and earrings.
Adorned with a great crown inlaid with infinite jewels, and joined with three hoods attached to the shimmering crown.
Each [face] was adorned with a great ruby shimmering upon the crown;
the three worlds were filled by the hissing breaths that emitted rays of light;
and it was beautiful with the downpour of nectar flowing from the orb of its moon-like face.
Having meditated upon [the deity] as Kulacaṇḍa, one should worship him three times with the mantra.
With the third *tāra* (OM) at the beginning and the end, and "Kulacaṇḍāya" in the middle,
this is declared to be the Kulacaṇḍa mantra, which bestows the command of Śambhu upon men.

Then, having resolved that all the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) shall serve as the *naivedya* (food offering), one should offer it from the side of the pavilion; thereafter, one should cast the *bali* offering upon the petals of the directions,
beginning with Yama, Kāmadhenu, and the best of mountains.
Then, on the petals starting from the tip and ending at the pericarp,
one should mentally recollect the four Siddhakanyakās; thereafter, one should release the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*) into the sky and place the vessel filled with food accompanied by side dishes.
One should sprinkle [the area] once with drops from the offering vessel (*arghyapātra*) of the conch.
Having drawn the *akatha* triangle and so forth, one should visualize an eight-petaled lotus around it.
Within the triangle, one should contemplate the four powers beginning with *bhuvana*, and in the center, *ya*...*
In the eight petals starting from the front, one should worship the group of eight beginning with Bāhmi.
In the directions of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, and Vāyu, as well as at the front, one should worship the four limbs (aṅgas).
One should worship the Mother Annapūrṇā along with her limbs and presiding deities.
Having offered the conch-water of honor to the guru, with his body sprinkled by that water,
he should then present the sandalwood paste, flowers, and other offerings to the guru in due order.
Having mentally drawn the remaining collection of atoms into the nectar of the *arghya*,
one should slowly lift the nectar remaining from the worship with both hands up to the head and place it upon the head as the mark of the Guru’s feet.
One should fill the entire manifest world of appearances with nectar;
then, one should transform that nectar into the Self.
One should consecrate the entire triad of principles with the root mantra.
One should bring a suitable maiden, or an auspicious married woman;
having worshipped her feet once, [one should offer] the vessel of the Goddess...
[the attendants] are present nearby.
The noble ones should offer them their esteem according to their own capacity and as is appropriate.
If, through negligence or forgetfulness, there has been an error in my speech— whatever has been uttered [in that regard]—
[may it be forgiven].
Together with the cause...
in some places [there is] the venerable Śrīkroḍabhaṭṭāraka...
the sage, having fallen from heaven, indeed becomes like ashes at that very moment.
At that very moment, the Lord of the Gods, having paid homage, spoke as follows:
"If you have the desire to protect the lineage of the Guru out of compassion,
please grant me the means of atonement and deliver me from the curse."
Intent upon its protection,
he first engaged in the churning of the Ocean of Milk after investigating the gods and asuras.
"Having made Mount Mandara the churning rod and Vāsuki the rope,
produce the nectar and, having taken possession of it for yourself, become pure.
Indra did exactly that in order to achieve the recovery of his own position."
At that moment, the Naga king, exhausted and unconscious,
fell helpless and was defiled by Time (Death).
At that very moment, he too was seen by me somewhere in such a state.
At the very moment he beheld him, he was awakened and fell under his power;
weeping with great flowers of praise while remembering me,
he then, out of compassion, related his former history right there.
"O Lord, since we are devoid of the assistance of a guru, of our own self-nature, and of a true companion, what recourse is there for us but you? You ought to lift us up out of compassion.
Therefore, I have exerted myself with great effort to rescue them."
Having become impossible to move due to the weight and impurity of his body,
he was lifted up with great effort by the strength of his arms and carried on the head;
likewise, the King of Nagas was satisfied, as was Bhava, the Lord of all.

Those who desire the fruits of their wishes for the year should perform the *pavitrāropaṇa* (the investiture of the sacred thread) during the period of the Lord’s sleep by means of the prescribed rites.
The King of Nagas seizes whatever merit that person has accumulated throughout the year who fails to perform the *pavitrāropaṇa* of the Teacher of the World during his sleep.
Then, having reflected upon that time, one should begin the rite of purification (*pavitravidhi*).
This should be done when the sun is situated in Cancer, Leo, or in the sign known as Virgo (*kanyā*).
On the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) is performed at night.
At dawn, following the completion of the daily obligatory rites, the ritual of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) takes place.
The cotton thread, as it may be obtained, should be washed with the dust from the roots [of the prescribed plants].
Having first multiplied by nine, and having further multiplied that according to the corresponding number,
one should bind it; hear its manifestation, O beloved,
which was formerly accepted as the principle of the logic of the Śrīśāmbhavāgama.
The sacred thread (*pavitra*) for the Guru is appropriate in two ways, depending on whether he is present or absent.
If the Guru is absent, it should be of the measure of nine finger-breadths;
if he is present, it should be of the measure of the lower garment. This is the settled rule.
Therefore, by joining the nine and the ten threads through the union of the manifest and the unmanifest,
and by means of the deity’s measurement, the wrapping cloth, and the accumulated [elements],
there is a single side with nine knots, nine threads, and nine finger-breadths.
One should wear a sacred thread (*pavitra*) with ten threads and ten knots when ten years of age;

however, regarding the number of threads for those aged two or more, no fixed rule exists here. Furthermore, for those who have served excellent gurus, there is a sacred thread consisting of five gurus.
The measurement for the deceased is declared according to the size of their lower garment;

[This applies] to the preparation of vessels, food offerings, sacrificial oblations, utensils, and so forth.
One should meditate upon the destinies according to their fitness;

In this Saubhāgyavidyācakra,
one should fashion the sacred threads (*pavitrāṇi*) with three knots for the [deities] beginning with Layāṅga and Avara.

the number of threads and the number of knots are as prescribed by the learned.

[One should offer] rice produced from *śāli* paddy that has been roasted in a sealed vessel (*puṭa*).

[This applies] to the two-eyed ones, the lords of the Āgamas,
the deceased, Gaṇanātha, Paṭuka, and the Guru as well.
One should worship the Devatāsūtras according to the rite of Śrīparā;
likewise in the fourfold purpose, and especially in the offering of bali.
Furthermore, [they are worshipped] in the context of Śrī, Sampat, Saṃvit, and thereafter in Saubhāgya.
One should worship, beginning with the three seats and ending with the bali offering;
and for the Goddess residing in the peace-vessel (śāntikumbha), one should worship with their respective mantras at the conclusion.
One should respectfully give threads to the officiating priests (ṛtvij) and the members of the assembly (sadasya).

Having consumed the lamp, one should complete the remainder of the sacrifice according to the procedure for the Great Sacrifice (mahāyāga), following the sequence of the fire-oblation (homa), the offering of bali, and so forth.
One should offer the purifying threads (*pavitra*) to Caṇḍā in their entirety, one after another in sequence.
Having offered incense, lamps, and so forth, one should present the great food offering (*mahānaivedya*).
After praying for the fruit of the year, one should dismiss Kulacaṇḍa.
One should wear those [threads] purified by His grace according to the appropriate rule. This procedure for the *pavitra* has been declared; one should apply whatever was not explicitly stated.
O Goddess, now hear in brief the ritual for the offering of *damanaka*.
On the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, at night, when the moon is in Taurus or Aries,
one should perform the ritual with the sacred *damanaka* grass according to the rules and with due skill.
Having carefully extracted it again and again by relying on the external shadow, one should prepare the vessel.
One should offer [the oblation] to the deities stationed in the pavilion of command (*ājñāmaṇḍapa*).
Then, one should meditate upon the lord of serpents named Caṇḍa in the *svādhiṣṭhāna* [cakra].
Having brought [the offering] from there, one should present everything before him.

Thus has been described the internal [rite] known as Pavitra and Damana. Without knowing these, one who performs both the external and internal [rites] incorrectly shall have a short life due to the curse of the Guru and shall experience bodily existence in hells such as Raurava.
Therefore, one who desires the accomplishment of all those mantras should diligently undertake the external and internal rites— both daily and occasional— in accordance with the proper method.
How many festival observances are there in a year for those seeking spiritual fruit?
The Caitra festival, the Pavitra, the Śayana, the Utthāna, and the Guru-parva—
these are the five rites here for those who perform their daily duties.
One should practice the "arising" (utthāna) during the sun's transit into the month of Makara;
one should offer the past time, along with sacred flowers, as before.
Likewise, during the sun's transit into the month of Karkaṭa, there is the "reclining" (śayana).
When rising, the worship is twofold; when lying down, it is fourfold.
For this very reason, those seeking liberation remain in meditative absorption during the four-month period.
The fifth festival has thus been described in brief; it cannot be fully detailed.
The two parvans (auspicious occasions) of the Guru’s birth and his passing away are well known. When there is an excellence of consciousness, that is called a parvan because of its fulfillment.
Indeed, while the Guru is living, the parvan is the day of attaining the status of a son.
That [initiation] is declared in the Śiva-scripture to be for the attainment of enlightenment.
One should perform that rite on the anniversary of the [disciple's] birth within the pervasive [tradition].
Now hear about initiation through mantras and so forth, for the purpose of establishing the [disciple's] birth and ritual status.
First, one should examine the disciple and the characteristics of the guru.
The supreme knowledge is bestowed, whereby sin is destroyed.
That initiation is Śāmbhavī, Māntrī, and Śāktī, according to the words of the Kula tradition.
Through the state of being adorned with earrings on the hundred-footed [body], one should gradually discern her;
Śāmbhavī, born from the two feet, bestows swift accomplishment.
The Mantra-deity [is worshipped] through the differentiation of the mantra...
one should draw an eight-petalled lotus surrounded by a square enclosure (*bhūgṛha*). One should write the *pūrṇa* [syllable] in the corners and the weapon (*astra*) in the cardinal directions.
Having worshipped him thoroughly with perfumes and other offerings,
one should install there Satyavān together with his wife, who is endowed with compassion.
One should purify [the area] by sprinkling the water from the conch-offering and the drops remaining in the vessel of worship.
One should cause the disciple to take a mouthful of water with the three *tattvas* out of a desire to perceive [the deities].
Then, one should contemplate [the disciple's] head and so forth.
One should worship those two, who possess the characteristics as previously described, with *dūrvā* grass and other offerings.
One should strike the head a hundred times with flowers previously consecrated by mantra.
With a mind from which the darkness has been dispelled by the multitude of spreading rays [of light],
one should drench [the deity] with drops from the vessel of worship, saturated with the nectar of mantra.

One should touch the heart-consciousness with a glance of compassion; having drawn it forth with the hand, one should impart the appropriate succession of mantras. Having consumed the lamp and the remainder of the sacrifice, one should properly complete everything.
Thus has been declared the essence of the procedure for initiation, as is fitting for the venerable Śāmbhava tradition.
This secret knowledge must be guarded with great effort.
The day of that initiation, whether it occurs monthly or even annually,
one should understand all of that as before and perform it as a duty.
I shall describe another method regarding the festival days and likewise for the Guru.
In the various treatises on guests, that which is declared as the *śrāddha* rite is to be understood as being of three kinds, according to whether it pertains to the deceased or the living:
[the offering] with the words "May the deceased [be pleased]," or with the words "May the living be pleased."

"May there be Bhairavas [in the portions]... [and so on]. When such a portion belongs to the Preceptor (*deśika*), he should speak thus during the night preceding the festival (*parvan*), following the sequence of the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
The consecration of the jar (ghaṭapratiṣṭhā) should be performed for the occasion of the Śrāddha rite;

having performed it like the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana), one should complete the remainder on a Saturday. One should invite [the guests] at early dawn with full elaboration according to one's means.

Having performed the daily and occasional rites, as well as the sequential extraction along with its proper order, one should [initiate] a paternal uncle, a noble father, a male practitioner (yogin), or a female practitioner (yoginī); or a young boy, a young girl, one's own disciple, or even one's own son.
Having performed the ritual for the family lamp, one should seat the invited guests.
One should worship them with flowers, scents, and so forth, as well as garments, finger-rings, and ornaments.
While touching the vessel with the left hand, [one should offer] with the right hand.
Having taken sesame water together with a sprout and accompanied by a ritual fee,
one should thus remember the glorious Guru-Natha while enshrining him within the mantra.
Having given the vessel, one should then distribute the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other items according to one's desire.
Then, having offered betel leaf, mouth-fresheners, and so forth, one should pray:
"May this first [rite] of the funeral (*antyeṣṭi*) and the ancestral festival (*śrāddha*) and others be performed."
Having consumed the lamp that remains from the sacrifice, one should worship as before.
Thus, the fivefold duties for the festival days have been briefly illustrated. The great festival (mahāparva) should be performed according to the proper method and at the appropriate time.
There are many gurus who exist throughout the kalpas and manvantaras.
For each of them, the festival (parvan) must be observed according to their specific times.
If the worshipper is unable to perform them at those respective times, [he should do so otherwise].
At one and the same time, however, there were eighteen gurus:
the eight beginning with Asitāṅga, as well as the four Nāthas—
Ciñciṇīśa, Caryānātha, and Mīnanātha as the third.
The illustrious Guru and Durvāsas— these four are indeed the lords of the three Vedas,
the two words, and the Yuga, though they appear in reverse order.
Likewise, the Lord Sadāśiva is the preceptor of the Manvantara.
The venerable Guru and the Kalpa-guru— these are the eighteen preceptors. Having prepared the coordination for the performance of the great festival,
they likewise perform on the preceding day the occasional rite known as adhivāsa.
Having performed [the preliminary rites] at dawn, one should invite the twenty-seventh [deity] through that yoga.
At dawn, after the completion of the daily duties, one should establish those who have been invited.
[With] garments, finger-...
[and so forth], one should fill [the space] with such splendor as is appropriate.
First, one should worship the Śāmbhava [deity] within the pericarp (karṇikā).
One should place Śrīparā, Śrīmahārthā,
and Śrīsampatsaubhāgyasampadā on the eight petals of the lotus of the Vedas (four petals), beginning with the white [petal] and so forth,
on both sides in both direct and reverse order.
Then one should worship Sadāśiva on the leaf, beginning with Durvāsas and ending with him;
thereafter, one should worship Śiva as the Preceptor of the Kalpa on the tip of the leaf. Then, one should worship Gaṇeśa in the direction of the Lord (the North) and Vaṭuka in the southeast corner.
One should worship the Śrī Guru in the south-western direction and Kuleśvarī in the north-west;
then, having established the sacrificial food (caru) according to the stated method, up to the end of the twenty-seventh [deity] and including the full oblation (pūrṇā),
one should first offer it as a presentation (nivedya) and subsequently give it along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
One should place eighteen lamps in a single vessel;
having prepared that same number of wicks, one should rotate them with the mantra consisting of eighteen aspects and offer them to the deities beginning with Asitāṅga and ending with Śiva.

Having uttered *hrauṃ* and *kṣraum*, one should recite "O Īśāna" and so forth at all the joints (*parva*). One should then utter the two seed-syllables in reverse order: "Grant me success, success" (*siddhiṃ siddhiṃ dehi*).
The eighteen-syllable mantra bestows the fruits of the great festivals (mahāparva).

One should worship it encased within the nine-fold self (navātma), separately with each of the eighteen Lords (nātha), and likewise worship the four beginning with Gaṇeśa with their respective mantras.
Thus ends the lamp-consecration with twenty-seven mantras recited previously.
Then, one should proclaim the yoga of the Great Wheel while beholding the lamp. And one should give to the poor during the half-day according to one's means.
Then one should complete the sacrifice; this is the ritual procedure for the great festival.
Thus [ends the work] composed by Śaṅkara, the embodied disciple of the venerable Somānanda.

The fourth daily lesson is completed with the composition of the *Padyavāhinī*. Indeed, the Goddess— who resides in the eye of the Sage (the Sun), who moves through the eyes of the Lord of the Mountain (Śiva) in due order, and who is the source of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and other qualities— having been enjoyed by Maṅgala and Bhallata, may she establish auspicious lines within the circle.
The wise one [should know] the ninefold group of the Nityānanda-cakra and the Jāticakra, which remove delusion, fulfill desires, agitate, bring fortune, protect wealth, and cure disease:
namely, desire (kāma), intellect (buddhi), ego (ahaṅkāra), sound (śabda), touch (sparśa), and form (rūpa).

One should employ sixteen mantras, beginning with *rasa*, *gandha*, *citta*, *dhairya*, and *smṛti*— these are the "seeded" (*sabījaka*) ones— and ending with *ātman*, *amṛta*, and *śarīra*. [The goddesses are] Kusumā, Mekhalā, Anaṅga, Madanā, and Madanāturā.
Rekhāvegī, Aṅkuśā, and likewise Anaṅgamālinī;
[they perform] agitation, dispersal, attraction, universal exhilaration, and delusion.
The [mantras] named Stambhana, Jambhana, Vaśīkaraṇa, Rañjana, and Unmādana;
those that destroy the pair of mantras which constitute the perfection of accomplishing one's purpose;
as well as Siddhisampat, Priya, Maṅgala, and likewise Kāmada.
It pacifies suffering and death, wards off all obstacles, and is beautiful in every limb.
It is the source of knowledge, power, and sovereignty; it is the support for wisdom, free from disease, and a purifier.
It is the protection of bliss and the fulfillment of desires, adorned with all excellences.
Kāminī, Bhaginī, Klinnā, Bhūruṇḍā, Vahnivāsinī, Vidyeśī, Dūtī, Tvaritā, Sundarī,
Sanatkā, Patākā, Vijayā, Maṅgalā, Jvālinī, and Citrikā.
Kusumā, Mekhalā, Anaṅgamadanā, Madanāturā,
Rekhāvegī, Aṅkuśā, and likewise Anaṅgamālinī—
[these women] were like a river of rut-fluid on the slopes of his hips, where intoxicated bees were submerged by the flow of their passion.
The hero, his bellowing greatly augmented by the expansion of his exceedingly sweet sound,
[is one who] has cast forth and disgorged lotuses from the tips of his own trunks...
[the leader].
May the elephant-faced one [Gaṇeśa] be for your prosperity— his form augmented by the swelling sounds of bees emerging from the ichor-fluid on his head, which has dispelled the calamity of obstacles.
Even though his eyes were covered by water,
the splendor of that body remained supreme due to the presence of the essence within its interior.
How many indeed are there, such as Brahmā and others, whose lordship is defiled by impurity and who are overcome [by obstacles]?
Only one remains, possessing firm accomplishment through his births.

O Tripurasundarī, he who performs even once the prostration at your feet, having once obtained your sidelong glance— which possesses a beauty blossoming with compassion— [attains all his desires]. (3)
Those who possess devotion, being truly blessed by the playful movements of Kandarpa, enchant even the young women throughout the three worlds.
Oṃ! The Vedas indeed chant your name as the syllable Oṃ.
O Mother, O Tripurā, dweller in the abode of the triangle, O three-eyed one!
Purified by you, the servants of Yama abandon their subjugation and sport in the palace of eternal bliss along with the world-protectors. (5)
How could the cruel force of the poison, which was being consumed as it reached the throat in order to kill [him] long ago,
not have become [intense] for your sake?
O Goddess, prostration at your lotus-feet produces omniscience and eloquence in the assembly for the Lord, who is as cool as a boat [to cross the ocean of existence]. 6.
He bestows a slightly shimmering crown, a radiant parasol,
two fly-whisks, and the great earth;
[he is] like wish-fulfilling trees in the granting of desired objects.
O Mother, O Tripurasundarī, look upon me with your nine ocean-like glances— me who am protectorless,
filled with devotion for you alone, and whose gaze is fixed upon you. (8)
Others, having directed their minds even toward those who are not devotees,
indeed carry out devotion toward base and ignorant people;
O Goddess, I alone remember you alone with my mind.
I bow to you alone as my refuge, O Mother; you alone [are my protection].
O Tripurasundarī, even though there are other targets for your glances, look upon me in some way with the light of your eyes.
Surely no person has ever been born, nor will one ever be born, who is my equal— a sole vessel for compassion.
(Your name is uttered by those) chanting "hrīṃ hrīṃ" at every step.
What indeed is difficult to obtain here in the residence of Tripura?
For Lakṣmī herself, full of sweetness, serves her who is honored by the intoxicated female elephants [of the quarters] wearing garlands and crowns. (11)
O lotus-eyed one, your glances bring prosperity, delight all the senses, bestow sovereignty, and are auspicious;
they are intent upon removing the distress of those who behold you.
May those [eyes] of the Lord Khandaparaśu, the Supreme Bhairava, who performs the Tāṇḍava dance at the conclusion of the aeons, gaze upon me alone incessantly, O Mother. (12)
Holding a noose, a goad, a sugarcane bow, and flower-arrows— may that singular splendor of yours, which bears witness [to all],
be victorious! O Mother, let this assembly be the target for you.
It is a supreme radiance, red as thick saffron paste,
adorned with a shining crown and an ornament of a digit of the moon;
it arises in the center of the triangle, known by the name of the Supreme Nectar.
O Mother, that knower of mantras who daily recites this hymn within your city— having kindled it with the great mantra encapsulated by the three *hrīṃ*syllables—
will find that his fortune becomes subject to him and remains stable for a long time.
His speech, filled with the weight of pure and well-spoken verses, remains awake for a long life;
his garland of letters is auspiciously adorned... [and so forth].
